en: Now begins the *Bṛhaddevatā* of Śaunaka.
Having paid homage to the seers of the mantras in their traditional sequence,
I shall declare the deities of the hymns, the half-verses, and the quarters of the verses according to the Ṛgveda.
One should diligently ascertain the deity for each mantra;
for one who knows the deities of the mantras understands their true purpose. (2)
The higher knowledge makes known those derivative meanings intended by the seers within their visions of the mantras, as well as various ritual actions.
For no one, without knowing the deity according to its true nature, enjoys the fruit of worldly or Vedic actions. (4)
Of these, the first group worships Agni as the deity here;
the second, Vāyu or Indra; and the third, Sūrya alone. (5)
When a seer, desiring a specific object, praises a particular deity with devotion—saying "May this one be so"—primarily through that mantra, that deity alone is [the object of the mantra]. (6)
Praise (stuti) is expressed by means of name, form, action, and kinship;
whereas benediction (āśis) is said to consist of objects such as heaven, long life, wealth, and sons. (7)
However, those *ṛc* verses in which praise (*stuti*) and benediction (*āśis*) are observed are few here;
and those in which heaven (*svarga*) is entreated would be even fewer than those two. (8)
He knows that everyone who praises him desires something from him;
and he perceives me as one who praises for a purpose, seeing me as having an object.
Whether by means of praise or by means of direct statement, both have been spoken by the seers who perceive reality;
for in their true meaning, both are equal.
One should recognize that very deity in a mantra by the perfection of its characteristics, in which the deity is directly mentioned.
Therefore, one who knows the application [of mantras] should diligently observe the plurality of the designations of the deities by their names in each individual mantra. || 12 ||
A complete statement of a seer is called a *sūkta*;
it is that in which a deity is perceived in one, in many, or in two [verses]. (13)
The diversity of deities, seers, meanings, and meters arises;
indeed, as many hymns as there are in a seer’s *sūkta* constitute the praise of a single [deity]. (14)
All those [verses] are heard as the hymn (sūkta) of that seer;
they call that "the hymn of meaning" (arthasūkta) which extends as far as the completion of the subject matter. 15.
A hymn (*sūkta*) is said to consist of verses that share the same meter; one should understand the diversity of hymns here exactly as it is. 1.6.
The names of deities in the mantras are indeed of three kinds:
those that receive the hymn (sūktabhāk), those that receive the remainder (avaśiṣṭabhāk), and likewise those that are incidental (naipātika). || 17 ||
Indeed, those containing *sūkta*s are called *sūktas*, and those containing *ṛc*s are called *ṛcs*;
some others mentioned here are recited with mantras dedicated to different deities. (1.8)
Whether by virtue of sharing the same world (sālokya) or by association (sāhacarya), those [names] are indeed derivative;
therefore, even though the hymn is of many kinds, it may still partake in the nature of a *sūkta*.
In that case, the deity is understood from the hymn (sūkta) as it is, without further distinction;
however, when the hymn is divided, one should state the deity here according to its indicative mark (liṅga).
In each respective case, one should employ the mantras appropriately for the rituals; for through the thorough knowledge of the deity, that ritual indeed succeeds. (21)

However, because the names of the deities are proclaimed by the reciters at the beginning and end of the hymns (*sūkta*) as part of the context, the knower of mantras should disregard them here. Regarding this, they indeed say: "From how many ritual acts does a name arise?"
Whatever belongs to living beings, whether they follow the Vedas or otherwise, whatever else exists here—|| 23 ||
The etymologists, the ancients, and those who are poets maintain that there are nine;
Madhuka, Śvetaketu, and Gālava likewise hold this view.
[He is so called] because of his dwelling, his actions, his form, his auspiciousness, his speech, his blessings,
his voluntary fasting, and likewise because he is the son of that [unknown] man.
Regarding the phrase "from four [suffixes]," Yāska, Gārgya, and Rathītara say therein that it refers to benedictions, or due to the diversity of meaning, or to speech, and indeed to action. (26)
Śaunaka has said that all these names arise from action; for the benediction, the form, and the object of speech—all become so through action. (27)
That which arises from fasting at will, as well as that which comes from being the son of another's wife—that too is indeed action; hear now the reasons for this. (28)
For living beings arise from karma; through karma comes the association with sentient beings.
Somewhere a being is born, and from that dwelling, offspring are produced.
But when a name is mentioned arbitrarily anywhere, one should understand that it arises from a comparison with some particular entity here in this world. (30)
For there is no entity that is without action, nor is there any name that is devoid of meaning;
names do not exist apart from entities, and therefore all [names] arise from action.
Whatever is performed for the sake of auspiciousness (maṅgala), and whatever arises from fasting (upavāsana)—
that indeed becomes a blessing (āśis) here, such as "svasti" and other forms of auspiciousness.
"How could this one with such a contemptible name live long here?"—thus are names assigned to beings, even when they are already well known. (33)
There are various kinds of mantras that have been perceived by the seers of mantras,
through praise and through the manifestation of power arising from the majesty of the divine Self.
Praise, eulogy, censure, doubt, lamentation, longing, benediction, boasting, begging, questioning, command, and the *pravahlikā* (the "what-if" or hypothetical). 35.
Injunction and inquiry, praise and lamentation, the desire to explain, conversation, and the narration of sacred accounts—these are [the topics]. (36)
Āhanasyā, Namaskāra, and likewise Pratirādha;
Saṃkalpa, Pralāpa, and similarly Prativākya. (37)
The prohibition and the instruction, the concealment of negligence, and that which is called the summons, as well as the fever and the wonder; (38)
Reproach and praise, as well as censure and likewise a curse;
the prefix and the particle, and also the noun and the verb. (39)
The past, the present, and the future; the male, the female, and the neuter—such are the types of mantras found everywhere in all the Vedas.
Certain verses, half-verses, and words intended for the perception of the meaning of a sentence are recited here both in the Brāhmaṇa and in the Kalpa.
The wise say that when a substance is understood through a word uttered here, that [word] is appropriately called a "name" (nāman) according to the rule for syllables.
That in which eight case-endings (vibhakti) are employed for various meanings is called a "noun" (nāman) by poets, even when there is a difference in number and gender. || 43 ||

That which, though consisting of many actions occurring in temporal sequence, is here a single entity established by virtue of the completion of those actions, they call the "meaning" expressed by a verb. (44)

When that which has arisen through the power of the actualization of an action is expressed by a word ending in a primary suffix (kṛt), and is joined with number, case-endings, indeclinables, and gender, then that state (bhāva) should be perceived as if it were a substance (dravya). || 45 ||
Just as the sages of old perceived through various sounds, listen now in due order to those diverse utterances found here. 46.

Praise is said to consist of [words concerning] form and so forth, while benediction likewise consists of [words concerning] heaven and so forth; whatever other sentences there may be besides these, they too would be of many kinds. (47)

In the *mantre* there is praise of Bhoja; in the *citra* of Sobhari there is a hymn of praise; but those [verses] beginning with "mātā ca" are seen to have the sense of reproach, as she addresses him with taunts. (48)

The Ṛg verse "ṛṅ mogham annam" refers to censure; the curse is expressed by "yo me"; the Ṛg verse itself is "yāñcā yad indra citra"; and the dismissal is expressed by "abhīdam" in the context of the skin.
The benediction is "May the wind blow [favorably]," while "O staff! is an expression of lamentation;
the question and the reply, "I ask you," are two separate verses. (50)
"Was there indeed a lower [world], or was it boastfulness?
'I am Manu'—the application of this [verse] to the phrase 'this sacrifice of ours' is called a quarter-verse. (51)
In this context, *anuyoga* (inquiry) is expressed by *bravītu*; *saṃlāpa* (conversation) by *ṛgupopa me*;
while *pratiṣedha* (prohibition) and *upadeśa* (instruction) are expressed by *akṣaiḥ* and *mā iti*, respectively, as they are praised for their non-sensory nature.
The narrative concerns the birth of a horse; there is the lamentation of Nala for his wife.
The praise of himself as one who has no hero (to protect him) expresses his longing for Sudeva. (53)
Salutations to Śunaḥśepa; salutations be to you, O Lightning!
That which is said when one forms this resolve, "May I become equal [to him]," [is here addressed]. (54)
"Saṃkalpa" is that which Indra said; "pralāpa" is that of Etaśa;
"mahānagni" and "ahanasya" would be [the forms]; "pratirādha" and "bhuk" as well. (55)
But negligence is this: "I am the slayer, not he," which is a denial;
"Indra, do not strike! is the preliminary command; and "I do not know" is the fever of remorse. (56)

"Hotṛ, let him sacrifice"—this is the *praiṣa* (direction); "Who indeed?"—this is the *vismaya* (expression of wonder). "Concealment from the sister"—this is the *pravalhikā* (enigma) beginning with "she is not stretched out. (57)
They relate this desire to explain [the state] where "death did not exist":
"May you be childless"—this was the curse; "May it be well with you," O Gautama—this was the blessing. (58)
Indeed, even much of this kind can be seen as such;
one may speak thus regarding their application based on the *ṛc*, the *sūkta*, and the *ardharca*. (59)
These mantra-sentences, however, resort to the deity who is the recipient of the hymn according to the proper rule; in this case, the praise is indeed inferential.
Some know the Sun alone to be the source and the dissolution of this world—of that which has been, of that which is to be, and of all things moving and stationary. (61)
This Prajāpati is the source of both the non-existent and the existent;
he is that which is the imperishable and that which is expressed by speech—this eternal Brahman.
For having divided himself threefold, he abides in these worlds,
having established all the gods, each in their proper place, within his own rays.
This fire-element, existing in three ways among the beings in the worlds,
the seers worship with hymns, manifested by means of its three names.
For he dwells within the belly of every living being as a blazing fire;
and those who have spread the sacrificial grass worship him in his three abodes during the oblation.
In this world, this Agni Pavamāna is the middle Agni, the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati);
whereas in that world, the Brahmin is called the pure Agni (Agni Śuci). || 66 ||
Here on earth he has become Agni, praised by the ṛṣis with hymns;
Jātavedas is praised in the midst, and Vaiśvānara is praised in heaven.
Having taken up the essences with his rays, he has gone forth together with the wind;
and because he rains upon the world, he is remembered as Indra.
"Agni is in this [earth], Indra is in the middle, and Vāyu as well;
Sūrya is in heaven—these three alone are to be known as the deities here. (69)
It is precisely due to their majesty that a difference in names is prescribed;
this is seen here in various places according to the division of those respective locations. (70)
This is indeed their manifestation, which the poets call by many names; yet in the mantras, they declare that these [names] are mutually born from one another.
These deities have been assigned to their respective places under different names;
some who are devoted to them and for whom they are primary speak of them in this way. (72)
Those three lords of the worlds and so forth who were previously mentioned separately—
their very self is all that which is proclaimed as devotion.
They say that his weapon is indeed splendor, and whatever may be his vehicle;
thus have these divine words, both addressed to Indra and uttered separately, been praised.
In those hymns of praise to many deities as well as those in praise of pairs of deities, the preeminence belongs exclusively to the husbands even therein. (75)
While performing the praise of the deity—repeating the names, the epithets, and the praises—he should disregard whatever worldly prosperity may arise here. (76)
One should conclude all offerings dedicated to Agni within the fire itself;

that which is dedicated to Indra, in Indra; and that which follows Sūrya, in Sūrya. Whatever oblation is prepared for a deity, and whichever deity a hymn (sūkta) is devoted to—[that deity is the recipient].
That alone would be the primary factor there, not that which is praised by a particle.
Thus has the summary rule for these three been stated;
having been thus explained in brief, the detailed sequence [will follow]. (79)
Indeed, the entire expansion of names must necessarily be understood;
for without knowing the names, the mantras cannot be understood. (80)
And even the bodiless beings, as well as the gods and great seers, praised [her] here with their respective powers through various hymns of praise. 81.
But by those [deeds] through which Agni, Indra, Soma, Vāyu, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, Candra, Viṣṇu, Parjanya, Pūṣan, the Ṛbhus, and the Aśvins [are attained]. (82)
The two worlds, the Maruts, the gods, the earth, the waters, Prajāpati, and the two gods Mitra and Varuṇa—both of them separately and together. || 83 ||
And all the gods, Savitṛ, and Tvaṣṭṛ— who is considered the creator of forms—
the horse, food, the officiating priests, the thunderbolt, and the pressing-stones yoked to the chariot,
were each praised individually with their own hymns, Ṛg-verses, and names.
In each successive hymn, I shall proclaim those [names] to you in their proper order.
One should determine that the mantra belongs to Agni by the characteristic marks of Agni,
by the primary offerings consisting of rows of oblations, and by the names and invocations alone.
But the mantra of Indra is characterized by the indicative marks (liṅga) of Vāyu and Indra, as well as by the names of the thunderbolt, its powerful actions, and its strength. (87)
But the *saurya* hymn partakes here of the indicative marks of Sūrya, all his solar qualities, his fiery attributes, and those names by which the hymn to Candra is characterized. (88)
By reciting the names of these deities,
however many there may be here for each individual, they do not fail to determine [the result] otherwise than this.
This is the application of these luminaries as they move through the three worlds; a wise knower of mantras does not falter in its application. (90)
Since this one is led by men, and since that one leads them, therefore these two performed actions of the same name, each separately. (91)
For whatever exists as already born, or whatever exists here as yet to be born—by means of that, these two worlds, bearing the same name, are both attained. || 92 ||
Showering these [missiles], this central one shines in the sky;
thus, some of the fiery [weapons] are described merely by their discharge. (93)
This Agni, the middle one, is Keśin by means of his flames and lightnings;
but that [sun] is Keśin by means of its rays; for this reason, he called them the Kaiśinas.
However, among these three Keśins individually,
three Keśins are observed here in the ritual procedures within the Ṛgveda.
Neither their origin, nor their manifestation, nor their birthplace can be described;
for by them this entire world is pervaded. (96)
For Agni has resorted to Vaiśvānara, and Vaiśvānara has resorted to Agni;
Jātavedas belongs to these two, and likewise these two belong to Jātavedas.

Because they share the same world, because they are born from the same source, and because of the pervasiveness of their splendor, each of them possesses divinity here; moreover, they are seen praised separately.
We say that the one who possesses the *sūkta* addressed to Agni is the terrestrial [Agni];
when the *sūkta* addressed to Jātavedas is mentioned, the intermediate [Agni] is traditionally taught to be therein. (99)
However, whenever we say "pertaining to Vaiśvānara," or wherever it may be, one should know that Sūrya is the recipient of the hymn when there is praise of Vaiśvānara. (100)
The two fires born of the Sun were seen in the midst of the earthly [fires] at every sacrifice of these very three worlds. (101)
Desiring to perform the *agnimāruta* śastra by descending from the ascent,
he begins it with the *vaiśvānara* hymn.
Then, however, he praises the deities of the middle position: Rudra and the Maruts in the first *stotriya*, and this Agni again in the second. (103)
Just as this has been stated regarding the origin of these places of manifestation,
so too is it seen here in various places concerning the God of gods.
If the locus of earth here is dependent upon fire,
then understand all of that as it is being described in due order.
Jātavedas indeed rests in Agni; Vaiśvānara rests in Agni;
likewise Draviṇodas and Idhma rest in Agni, as does Tanūnapāt.
Narāśaṃsa has resorted to him, and Tilvila likewise has resorted to him;
Barhis and the goddesses of the doors have indeed taken refuge in this very Agni. || 107 ||
Night and Dawn, the two divine Hotṛ-priests, have taken refuge in him;
the three goddesses have taken refuge in him, and Tvaṣṭṛ likewise has taken refuge in him.
The lord of the forest (the tree) rests upon him, as do the utterances of "svāhā";
likewise, the horse, the bird, and the frogs have this as their refuge.
The pressing-stones, the dice, the Narāśaṃsa, as well as the chariot, the drum, the quiver, the hand-guard, the reins, and the bow—these attend him. (110)
The bowstring and the arrows resting upon it, the whip and the horse,
the bull and the mallet, and the father and the mortar— each of these has resorted to this very one.
The rivers, the waters, and all the herbs;
Night, Apvā, Agnāyī, Araṇyānī, Śraddhā, Ilā, and likewise the Earth—[all these attend upon him]. || 112 ||
The two Apsarases Rodasī, who exist as a pair, worship him;
and those known as Musalolūkhalā worship him, as do the two Havirdhānas.
Joṣṭrī and Urjāhuti, along with the Śutudrī and the Vipāś, as well as the two gods Śuna and Sīra, and the two fires (Agnis) that depend upon them—all these [attend him]. 114.
This world is indeed that which is performed as the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) in the sacrifice;
the two seasons, spring and autumn, are its stoma, the Anuṣṭubh meter, and the Trivṛt chant. || 115 ||
The Gāyatrī and the twenty-one-fold hymn, the Rathantara Sāman, the Sādhyas with the Vairāja Sāman, and the Āptyas together with the Vasus. || 11.6 ||
There is a hymn of praise to him by Indra, the Maruts, Soma, Varuṇa,
Parjanya, the Seasons, and Viṣṇu.
One who knows the true nature of the deities should, by means of mantras, join this very oblation with Agni, Pūṣan, and Varuṇa for the sake of sovereign power. 118.
Even for one who is a stranger, a single oblation is prepared;
likewise, there is the invocation of the deity and the offering of the oblations. (119)
Whatever action revolves within the objects of the visible world—
all this great host has been described as having the earth and fire as its support.
Beyond this is the host that occupies the intermediate space, belonging to Indra.
And there were divine celestial chariots, as well as a host of apsarases.
Parjanya, Rudra, Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Ka, Mṛtyu, and the god Brahmaṇaspati have Indra as their refuge. || 122 ||
Manyu, Viśvakarman, Mitra, Kṣetrapati,
Yama, Tārkṣya, Vāstoṣpati, and Sarasvant are likewise present here.
Apāṃnapāt, Dadhikrā, Suparṇa, Purūravas, Ṛtu, Asunīti, and Vena; Aditi is the refuge of this very [group]. (124)
Tvaṣṭṛ and Savitṛ, Vāta and Vācaspati, as well as Dhātṛ and Prajāpati, and those who are remembered as the Atharvans. || 1.25 ||
Śyena, Agni, and likewise she who is remembered as Ilā;
Vidhātṛ, Indu, Ahibudhnya, Soma, Ahiratha, and Candramas. (126)
The divine Viśvānara and the host of Rudras are praised together,
as are the Maruts, the Aṅgirases, and the Pitṛs along with the Arbhus.
Rākā, Vāk, Saramā, Aptyā, Bhṛgu, Aghnyā, Sarasvatī, Yamī, Urvaśī, Sinīvālī, Pathyā, Svasti, Uṣas, and Kuhū. || 128 ||
He is Pṛthivī, Anumati, Dhenu, Sītā, Lākṣā, and likewise Gau; he is Gaurī, Rodasī, and indeed the husband of Indrāṇī. || 129 ||
One should know that the Triṣṭubh and Paṅkti meters, as well as that which is the middle of the worlds—these are the support for the middle pressing. || 130 ||
The seasons of summer and winter, that which is called the Bṛhat Sāman, and that which is sung upon the Śakvarī verses—by name, that is the Śākvara Sāman. (131)
Thus ends the first chapter of the Bṛhaddevatā.
And Śākaṭāyana has stated that its two supporting *stomas* are that which is named Pañcadaśa and that which is [named] Triṇava by number. (1)
He was praised by Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa;
by Soma, Vāyu, Agni, and Kutsa; and indeed by Brahmaṇaspati.
He who is also named Parvata was likewise praised by Bṛhaspati.
In certain cases, they say "some [people]," for these particles are praised in eulogies. (3)
And it is heard that the god Mitra was repeatedly joined with Varuṇa;
Soma with Rudra; and Pūṣan again with Vāyu.
And Parjanya is perceived through the wind alone, except in certain instances;
however, in these [passages] consisting of whole verses, half-verses, quarters, and hymns, it is perceived in its entirety.
The taking of the *rasa*, the slaying of Vṛtra, the mastery over all praise, and the entirety of his power—all this is his work. (6)
Thus has the middle-positioned group belonging to Indra been correctly described;
now learn that which is the subsequent group, belonging to Sūrya and situated in the celestial realm.
The two gods, the Aśvins, are his most eminent [offspring], residing in the sun;
Vṛṣākapāyī, Sūryā, and Uṣas are indeed the wives of the sun.
From that point they turn back toward this world; those who depend on her follow in reverse order.
Before sunrise, they call her Uṣas; when the sun is at midday, Sūryā;
and at sunset, Vṛṣākapāyī. They speak of her as being one and the same.
In her abode were Saraṇyū, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Vṛṣākapi. || 2.10 ||
Yama, Vaiśvānara, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Aja-Ekapāt;
the Earth and the Ocean; the gods and those who are the Seven Sages;
the Ādityas, Keśins, and Sādhyas; Savitṛ with the Vasus, and Manu. || 11 ||
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, all the Vājins, and the wives of the gods. || 1.2 ||
That is the third pressing (savana), the world, and the Rāyovājīya Sāman;
likewise the Vairūpa [Sāman], the rainy season, and the winter solstice (śiśira) as the season. || 13 ||
The hymn-form (stoma) consisting of thirty-three, that which consists of seventeen by arrangement, the metre named Jagatī, and likewise those which are Atichandas; || 14 ||
They say that all this is his human effort;
yet, it should be understood that the three gods are merely its laudatory designations.
The Moon, the Wind, and that which they know as the Year—
some indeed offer for him the oblation dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara.
For that hymn appears like one dedicated to Sūrya or Vaiśvānara, consisting of a single Ṛc, a half-verse, a quarter-verse, two verses, or even three verses. (17)
By this proclamation, however, praise is seen from one who possesses a head;
here, the identity of the Sun, Vaiśvānara, and Agni is perceived.
This is the withdrawal of the essence by means of its rays, both here and in the hereafter, whereby all beings do not perceive it with their eyes. (19)
One who correctly understands this classification of these [mantras], which arises from their respective states of power, should employ them in the ritual actions.
"By teaching, by studying, and by reciting the mantra, one attains their very station—be it sālokya or sāyujya. (21)
The poets say that there are five hymns (sūktas) for Agni consisting of his names,
twenty-six for Indra, and seven for Sūrya.
Listen as I explain to you, in their entirety and according to the proper method, the individual etymologies of each of these, which arise from their respective functions.
Since he was born at the beginning of all beings as their leader in the sacrifice, and since his body is brought together by name through praise as "Agni" by the wise, [he is so called]. (24)
Seeing that he bestowed wealth, riches, or even strength through such an act,
Kutsa addressed him as Draviṇodas (the Giver of Wealth).
This Agni is Tanūnapāt; for he is "tanu" because of his expansion.
From him was born the middle one, and this [middle one] arose from the middle place. (26)
Those who are compassionate say that the one immediately following a descendant is the *napāt*; and because this Agni belongs to that very *napāt*, he is therefore called *Tanūnapāt*.
That which is praised by men in the sacrifice through both individual and collective formulas—the singers praise that Narāśaṃsa with the Āprī hymns. (28)
Because this terrestrial fire purifies this entire universe, it is praised as Pavamāna by the Vaikhānasa sages. || 29 ||
He knows all beings once he is born; therefore, he is called Jātavedas.
Furthermore, because he has become possessed of knowledge upon birth, or because he perceives what is acquired once born, he is so named. (2.30)
For he exists within all beings, or rather, he is born again and again; therefore this Lord of the Middle Region is praised as Jātavedas. || 3.1 ||
Because he is the most subtle, being one who stands pervading the three [worlds] within the sky, the sages, honoring him through ritual action, called this Vāyu "Aṇimat. (32)
Because he alone covers these three with his embodied essence, those who are compassionate call this Varuṇa by that very power in their hymns of praise. (33)
Because he roared in the sky while bestowing lightning and rain upon men,
he was praised as Rudra by the four ṛṣis.
Having become the vital breath of the four kinds of beings, he presides over all this; therefore, he is remembered as Indra.
Because he split the earth (irā) at that time while in the sky accompanied by the Maruts and endowed with a great roar, the sages called him Indra. || 36 ||
Because Atri alone ploughed this earth with the seed of passion,
and Aurva did so at the proper time, those two sages are called Parjanya.
Because he satisfies the worlds, because he is a kinsman who benefits all people, and because he is the supreme conqueror and progenitor, he was therefore proclaimed as "Āgneya. (38)
Because he protects these two vast worlds—the middle and the highest—he is celebrated as Bṛhaspati on account of that great deed. || 39 ||
Brahman is speech, Brahman is truth, and Brahman is this entire world;
thus Śaunahotra sang in praise of the protector of Brahman.
Because he entered the earth during the seasons while bestowing food upon the lands, Vāmadeva praised him as the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati). 41.
But this middle world which is perceived by the mind, though he praised it as truth, he has in fact praised falsehood with truth. (42)
Having been cast into the interior of the sun by Ravaṇa through his illusory power, he remained stationed in the sky;
then he spoke to him again with this verse of the Ṛgveda: "The song of Truth... (Ṛgveda 10.89.4).
Because he bestows a dwelling upon the world and protects that which is in its midst, Aurvaśa addressed him as Vāstoṣpati with these four [verses].
For by speech the Vedas are studied, and by speech the meters exist therein;
moreover, speech is indeed all this. Therefore, Vācaspati is praised. || 45 ||
Because he remained in the middle, not dejected by anything whatsoever, the seer Rāhūgaṇa called him Gotama, and [the seer] Aditi called him [Gotama]. 46.
Desiring for his subjects that protection which he sought with his mind as happiness, the seer Hiraṇyagarbha, praising him, spoke thus: "To whom [do you belong]? (RV 10.121.1).
Because he goes forth after gathering and bestowing offspring here, the seer [Vaivasvata] called this son of Vivasvat Yama. || 48 ||
"Since all people, having made him their friend, sit around him, he himself praised him as 'Viśvāmitra' while addressing him as 'Mitra'. (49)
Because he protects the earth with truth when the month of Nidāgha has passed,
and because he brings about the activity of the universe, he is therefore called Viśvakarman.
In the three worlds, his lakes are full of clarified butter;
they call him Sarasvant, and they call Speech Sarasvatī.
Because he dwells within all beings as their vital breath,
the seer Vena— the Bhārgava known here by that name— therefore brought him forth from Vena.
Month after month, she gave birth to him, conceiving him as the foremost of ascetic power (tapas).
Therefore, he said to him, "You are Wrath (manyu)," for the ascetic was indeed Wrath himself.
Because at the time of the end of beings, he alone leads away their vital breaths,
for this reason he is called Asunīti by Śrutabandhu when offering praise.
At the end of the summer months, the birth of waters occurs in their midst;
for this reason, the seer Gṛtsamada, while praising him, called him "the grandson. (55)
Because he, assuming the form of a calf eight months old within the mass of waters in the midst of the sky,
cries out repeatedly, he is therefore called Dadhikrā.

Having been nurtured for nine months, the embryo, now at the ninth month, cries out as it is placed upon the earth by its own accord; thus he is celebrated in the Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "dhātā."
Because he dwells in the vast expanse of the sky, or because he flows swiftly,
this sage Ariṣṭanemi Tārkṣya spoke thus concerning Tārkṣya.
Crying out in the sky as he rose, shedding tears from his eyes, she, dwelling in the vast expanse, addressed him with her own words: "O Purūravas! (59)
But because he approaches the dead with a great roar, driving them away, he himself praises this very death as "Death. (2.60)
By name he was Saṃkusuka, the youngest son of Yama;
he was dispersing the darkness from the sun and bringing forth the dawn.
Having arisen and illuminating these worlds with his own rays, he shines by himself;
therefore, Vasiṣṭha, praising him as Bhaga, called him "Bhagavan."
Nourishing the earth and dispelling darkness with his rays, Pūṣan was praised by Bharadvāja with five verses as "Pūṣan. (63)
Because his three steps shine with splendor,
Medhātithi has called this Viṣṇu Trivikrama.
Having performed his evening rites, he goes apart from all beings at the end of darkness, making light with his rays; for this reason, they know him as Keśin.
Because men now regard him individually as being distinct from each one of them,
he is praised in hymns as Viśvānara by virtue of that action.

Since this bull, having become Kapila, ascends to the firmament, he is therefore Vṛṣākapi; thus Indra is supreme over the entire universe. Shaking [the world] with his rays, that bull indeed moves as the most exalted one.
That at the time of evening he sets while putting all beings to sleep—this is seen in the mantras as "vṛṣākapi" or "itaḥ. (68)
In the *Dhanu* hymn, he is indeed addressed as "Indra" by Vāriṣākapi.
Viṣṇu is so defined from the roots *viṣ*, *viś*, or *vevī*, meaning "to pervade";
thus the Sun is called Viṣṇu, for he is everything and that which dwells within all. (69)
The names of Agni, Indra, and Sūrya are correctly stated to be five, twenty-six, and seven respectively.
However, for the nouns formed by nominal suffixes (*naipātika*), because they are endowed with the previously stated characteristics of nouns, no separate enumeration exists. (71)
Speech is threefold: that of the earth, that of the intermediate space, and that of heaven;
learn now its well-spoken names according to their respective places.
This river, when praised on earth, enjoys the entirety of the well-spoken hymn;
so too when the waters, the plants, and [the other elements] attend upon it. (73)
Although she is Agnayī by name, she is seen here in various places praised merely as a nipāta (an inserted particle) within certain passages dedicated to Agni.
In the middle, having become Satyaditi and Vāk, she is this Sarasvatī;
thus, through these three very names, she partakes of the entire hymn.
This very [goddess], having become Durgā and performed worship, becomes a partaker of the hymn (sūkta).
Her names are Yamī, Indrāṇī, Saramā, Romaśā, Urvaśī, Bhavānī, Agryā, Sinīvālī, Rākā, Anumati, and Kuhū.
Gauḥ, dhenūḥ, devapatnyaḥ, aghnyāḥ, pathyā, svasti, rodasī, and naipātikāni—these are some of the names which possess the character of Ṛg-verses. (78)
But when this speech becomes Sūryā and has resorted to that world, then, having become Uṣas, she enjoys the entire hymn along with Sūryā. 79.
Having become the Vṛṣākapi verse, Saraṇyū remains firm in both;
though she is truly the earth, she partakes only in a metaphorical designation, just like the sky.
We indeed perceive this very Sūryā, the truthful Gaurī, Sarasvatī, solely through her appearance within the Vaiśvadeva hymns. 81.
Ghoṣā, Godhā, Viśvavārā, Apālā, Upaniṣad, Niṣat, Brahmajāyā named Jahū, and Aditi, the sister of Agastya. || 82 ||
Indrāṇī, Indramātā, Saramā, Romaśā, Urvaśī, Lopāmudrā, the rivers, Yamī, and the eternal Nārī. || 83 ||
Śrī, Lākṣā, Sārparājñī, Vāk, Śraddhā, Medhā, Dakṣiṇā, Rātrī, Sūryā, and Sāvitrī are declared to be the expounders of Brahman. (84)
The first group among them consisted of nine verses and praised the deities;
the middle collection was composed by both sages and deities. (85)
The highest class likewise sang of the dispositions of the self;
and the deity of that highest class is the very same as its seer (ṛṣi).
But that which is the highest Varga praises the Self as the deity;
therefore, in self-praises, whoever is the seer (ṛṣi), he alone is the deity.
In dialogues, he who speaks the words shall be the seer (ṛṣi) therein;
and whichever deity is expressed by those words, that deity shall be the one present there.
Particles (nipātas) are declared to be used for various high and low meanings, for the purpose of including an object, and sometimes by way of comparison. (89)
In some cases, other particles are used at the end of quarters [of verses] for the purpose of filling out deficiencies;
however, in works composed of measured syllables (mitākṣara), these are merely for the sake of filling the meter and are semantically meaningless. (2.90)

Those which signify "like" (iva) should be understood as *kamami* [particles]; however, those which have multiple meanings—namely, *cinnu*, *iva*, and *nu*—are four in number and serve the purpose of comparison (*upamā*). 91.
The particle *na* is employed in the sense of comparison only in certain instances; however, in concise treatises, it is used very frequently in the sense of negation. (92)
There is no enumeration of particles such that one could say "there are this many"; they are introduced at every step according to the requirements of the context. (93)
The prefixes, numbering twenty, should be understood as functioning through their connection with verbal roots;
for they distinguish the meaning within nouns, verbs, and inflections. (94)

Today, the teacher Śākaṭāyana considers these—*ati*, *adhi*, and *anu*—to be prepositions (*upasarga*) when they are joined with a verb; however, those [other prepositions] are three times more numerous. (95)
There are only three genders in the world: male, female, and neuter;
likewise, in the application of names and hymns, one must consider both the gender and the context. (96)
Their apprehension is by means of their names and characteristics, as well as by all pronouns;
there is a re-apprehension of what has already been apprehended, whether it be similar to what was done or left undone. (97)
Some call them "Pādas," "Sūktas," "Ṛks," "Half-verses" (Ardharcas), "Names," or whatever other names there may be; others likewise speak of them according to their own accounts.
For the word is held to have meaning as its primary function, while it is dependent upon that [meaning] as its quality;
therefore, one should bring words under the control of the meaning through various methods of syntactic connection. (99)
One should discard an excessive word or insert one that is deficient in the sentence; one should connect what is separated and arrange the proper sequence. (2.100)
In each respective case, one should adapt the gender, the root, and the inflection;
whatever may be Vedic in the mantra, that should be rendered into the common (laukika) form.

To whatever extent the gender of the elements has become conventional, and to whatever extent their meaning is to be expressed, the analysis of their qualities should be performed by that many [elements]. (102)

A word is characterized by its etymological derivation (*nirvācya-lakṣaṇa*); it may consist of a root, a prefix, a suffix, or a derivative quality-suffix, and it may be produced from two roots, many roots, or even a single root. (103)

A word is to be defined as fivefold: that which is born from a root-element (*dhātuja*), that which is born from what is born from a root-element (*dhātujājāta*), that which is born from the meaning of a whole [compound], that which is born from a sentence (*vākyaja*), and that which is intermingled (*vyatikīrṇa*). 104.
The Dvigu, the Dvandva, the Avyayībhāva, and the Karmadhāraya;
the fifth is the Bahuvrīhi, and the sixth is known as the Tatpuruṣa. (105)
Etymological derivation should be performed by analyzing the constituent parts of a compound, as well as those in nominal suffixes (*taddhita*).
Even in cases such as "one deserving punishment" (*daṇḍārha*) being derived as "one to be punished" (*daṇḍya*), the analysis must be carried out by breaking the word down into its components.
"His wife is beautiful" and "he has a beautiful wife"—in these cases, *indrāsoma* serves as the illustration, as in "Indra and Soma. (107)

The word-form, the meaning of the term, etymology, the root, and the quality—all these have multiple meanings; however, when there is no comprehension, they serve as subordinate factors (guṇas). || 108 ||
Words denoting a general category are sometimes established in a specific instance; for example, when fleeing, who indeed would desire the conduct of a "coward" (marya)? 109.
In some cases, however, other words denoting specific particulars are established in a general sense;
the word *hima* in the mantra "by cold [is quenched] fire" is an illustration of this. (2.110)
Having taken up the single word and divided it into two parts, Yāska explained the term *puruṣāda* as "on every tree" (*vṛkṣe-vṛkṣe*) and [the second part] as "in the bark" (*tvaci*). || 111 ||

The etymologist has explained "aruṇa" in two ways: sometimes as a single word and at other times as multiple words; sometimes it is used once within a mantra, and sometimes it is used twice with a distinct grammatical analysis.
Even when separated by other words, he explained them as a single compound in the verse:
"The womb, the treasure—these are not sisters" (RV 10.10.4).
In the verse "tvaḥ pade," the meaning of the word is not understood due to its morphological class (*padajāti*);
likewise, in the verse "vane na," the failure to perceive the vowels has been demonstrated. (11.4)
In the verses beginning with "śunaḥśepam," "narāśaṃsam," "dyāvā naḥ pṛthivī," and "niraskṛte," the sequence [of words] occurred according to their meaning. || 115 ||
There is elision of a single consonant, of two consonants, or of many consonants;
as in *atrāṇi*, *kapir nābhāt*, *danoyāmī*, and in the verses beginning with *aghāsu*.
From the meaning comes the word, which has its own denotation; from the word comes the determination of the sentence-meaning.
A sentence is born from a collection of words, and a word is born from a collection of phonemes.

The discernment of meaning in mantras arises from context, from the subject matter, from indicative marks, from propriety, and from place and time; such is the established rule for others as well. (11.8)
Thus, he who strives in etymology through various methods and means—even if he is a seeker of the nature of Brahman—shall go to the highest state despite his evil deeds. (1.1.9)
Just as this [world] did not exist at first—whether it was non-existent or even existent—they declare that to be the course of becoming by which all this was born. (2.120)
The verb denotes the primary state of being; there are six modifications of it:
birth, existence, transformation, growth, decay, and destruction. (121)

But as for those other modifications of being that arise from these very six, they should be inferred according to the statements [of the scriptures] by those most skilled in mantras through their own capacity. (122)
Likewise, through salutations to the gods and the ancestors—
whether performed individually or collectively— hear now the deities of the *vyāhṛtis*.
The deity of the *vyāhṛtis* taken together is Prajāpati;
of those taken individually, the deities are this Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya.
Is it the deity of speech, or perhaps Indra, or the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin)? Is the syllable Om belonging to all the gods, or to Brahmā, or to some other deity? || 125 ||
The first hymn is dedicated to Agni and is the seerly work of Madhuchandas; all the seven triplets following it are to be known as having other deities. 1.26.
Of these, the first is for Vāyu; the next is for Indra and Vāyu; then that for Mitra and Varuṇa, then that for the Aśvins, then that for Indra, and thereafter that for the Viśvedevas. || 1.27 ||
That which bears that name (vaiśvadeva), or that which contains universal characteristics, or the final triplet (tṛca) in the gāyatrī meter—
these, or any other [hymn] dedicated to many deities, are praised among the vaiśvadeva offerings.
To Luśa, Duvasyu, Śāryāta, Gotama, and then to Ṛjiśvan;
to Avatsāra, Parucchepa, Atri, and the seer Dīrghatamas—[to these] let [the hymn] be dear. 129.
In Vasiṣṭha, Nābhānediṣṭha, Gaya, Medhātithi, Manu, Kakṣīvat, and Vihavya, as well as among many other ṛṣis. ||2.130||
In Agastya, Bṛhaduktha, and Viśvāmitra Gāthin,
various conflicting accounts are seen here in their respective hymns of praise.
Regarding that mantra in which a convergence of many [deities] is observed, the two teachers Yāska and Śāṇḍilya have declared it to be Vaiśvadeva. (132)
Whether it be a quarter-verse, a half-verse, a single verse, or even a hymn, one should recite everything that pertains to the Viśvedevas or has many deities as its object. (133)
All the deities have been praised by the seers with all manner of hymns; however, this designation "Viśva" (the All) is employed in the sense of attaining everything. 134.
The seventh [deity] is Sarasvata; these are the deities of the Prauga-śastra. In all the ṛcs, she is praised under two forms as "Sarasvatī. (135)
In that matter, the teacher Śaunaka was like a river and like a deity;
he declared that the six Vedas are like rivers, while the seventh is not so.
Yāska, however, considered "ambyekā ca dṛṣadvatyām," "citra icca sarasvatī," and "iyaṃ śuṣmebhiḥ" as the seventh [sūkta]. (137)

In the Maitrāyaṇīyaka, [the author], seeing that this [verse] is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the animal sacrifice to Sarasvatī, declared it to belong to Speech alone, on account of the primacy of the oblation. || 138 ||
The hymn beginning with "surūpakṛtnum" is dedicated to Indra; there are seven other verses following it.
The six verses immediately preceding it are addressed to the Maruts, according to their own nature. (139)
Even though it is a single verse, it is sung for Indra together with the Maruts;
of that [verse], which has an interval of one [verse], the final half-verse belongs to two deities. (2.140)
Thus was Indra, the leader of the host of Maruts, questioned:
"Are [the two] slow (*manda*) and of equal luster, or are they slow and of great luster?
Those for whom [the deity] belongs to two deities (*dvidevatya*) pronounce [the name] as *mandū* with a protracted vowel.
Having recognized from study that a word [indicates] a single deity, one should cause the announcement (āśrāvya). || 142 ||

Just as Rodasī is among the wives of the gods and Atharvāṅgiras among the Atharvans, so too is this [Goddess] considered the foremost among the hosts of Maruts and the preeminent among the Teachers (Ācāryas). 143.
Because he is the foremost of the host of Maruts, Indra was indeed subject to doubt;
however, they know the entire host of Maruts to be equal in portion to Mahendra. (144)
The verse beginning with "agnim" has Agni as its deity; among its quarters, one has two deities.
Having produced fire by friction for the sake of the Āhavanīya fire, the fire is kindled by means of fire. (145)
"The first quarter-verse has Agni as its deity; the two [fires], the Nirmathya and the Āhavanīya, are produced by friction.
Now, in the second [section] consisting of twelve verses, listen to me as I name those deities who are praised along with Agni in each verse. (146)
If the *idhma* is praised in the first [verse], *tanūnapāt* in the second, *narāśaṃsa* in the third, then *tviṣ* is praised in the fourth. (147)
On the fifth day, however, [he recites] the *barhis* verse; then the goddesses of the doors with the next [verse];
on the seventh day, the *naktoṣāsā*; and on the eighth day, the two [verses] are recited together.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests are praised in the ninth verse;
the three goddesses are praised in the tenth, while Tvaṣṭṛ alone is to be known as the one praised [therein]. || 149 ||
On the eleventh day, one should know that the Vanaspati is praised in the Sūkta;
on the twelfth day, one should know that the Svāhākṛtis, the goddesses, are praised.
Whatever deities are proclaimed in each verse (ṛc) of this hymn (sūkta), those very same ones [are the deities] in all the Āprī verses; however, the second [verse] is subject to option. 151.
Together with the *praiṣas*, there are eleven *aprīsūktas*;
however, these others consist of either *yajus* formulas or *praiṣasūktas*, numbering ten.
The three Sautrāmaṇī [offerings] are in the Prājāpatya and Aśvamedha;
those in the Puruṣamedha are among the Yajus-mantras alone—thus there are six.
In this very context, there should be a *praiṣa-sūkta*; one should not pay heed to those [verses] among the *yajus* formulas.
Among them, the *sūkta* contained in the *praiṣas*, which Dīrghatamas sang, [is what is intended]. (154)
And that which was said regarding Medhātithi—"only three [stanzas] possess both [characteristics]"—and that which is stated concerning the seer Gṛtsamada and Vādhryaśva; || 155 ||
He beheld that which was praised by Narāśaṃsa and Atri, and that which Aurvaśa saw;
and that which Tanūnapāt, Agastya, and Jamadagni sang.
The seer Viśvāmitra and Asita Kāśyapa sang [the hymns], as well as those twelve deities mentioned in the verses of Medhātithi. (157)
Understand that perfection which results in them becoming like fire:
the fuel is the entire fire itself, for this very fuel is kindled.
This form indeed belongs to the root *dhmā*; for fuel (*idhma*) is kindled when it is blown upon. || 158 ||
Thus ends the second chapter of the Bṛhaddevatā.
"He is indeed Tanūnapāt by name because he does not abandon (na apādat) his body; they call him 'Prajā' because of his origin from that [Supreme Being]. (1)
Some here call Agni "Narāśaṃsa," while others say it is because all men praise him as he sits at the sacrifice.
Others call this very fire Narāśaṃsa in the sacrifice;
for he is praised by men seated [there], and the priests call him "Nara. || 3 ||
I praise the form created by Ilā; from the root *iḍ*, meaning "to praise," Agni is called *ilāvān* because he is increased by that which possesses praise (*iḍin*), namely the act of increasing.
This fire is indeed the sacrificial grass (barhis), for it is entirely nourished by food; whether it is struck down or present, it is strengthened by the fuel-stick (idhma). || 5 ||
The two goddesses who were mentioned as the gatekeepers are the wives of all the Viśvedevas;
they follow Agnāyī, and likewise Agnāyī follows Agni himself.
Established as constant within the fire, they are praised together with Agni;
what preeminence, then, can there be for Agni alone in these hymns and in the sacrificial offerings? (7)
And the two goddesses, Night and Dawn, are remembered as being of the nature of Agni;
for Śyāvī is of the nature of Agni, while Uṣas is indeed like a digit of that very Time.
Dawn dispels the darkness, and Night [dispels] this [darkness] with drops of frost;
or rather, this may be derived from the root *añc* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, meaning "of indistinct color. (9)
For she is called *Doṣā* (Night) at the beginning; at midnight she is *Tamasvatī* (Full of Darkness); and by the name *Uṣā* (Dawn) she is known before the rising of the sun. || 10 ||
The two Hotṛ priests, however, are the two divine Agnis, the terrestrial and the intermediate;
for they were born from the celestial Agni, and thus they are called "divine" (daivya) because of this birth.
The three goddesses who have been mentioned are indeed that Speech (Vāk) abiding in three places;
she is expressed by a threefold name as she dwells within the three lights.
But the Sarasvatī, having followed after Agni and reached the middle [region], becomes Bhāratī in this world where she stands. (13)
This very speech, indeed, is threefold—both in heaven, in the intermediate space, and here on earth;
whether distributed or unified, it partakes of these fires as well.
But as for Tvaṣṭṛ, he is praised as being this very terrestrial fire; the splendor of this terrestrial [fire] is found in certain Ṛks among the seasonal hymns. (15)
It may derive from the root *tviṣ* (to shine) or *takṣ* (to fashion); or it may mean "he who eats grass" (*tṛṇam aśnute*);
or it means "the deliverer from karma" (*karma-sṛt-tāraṇaḥ*). By this, he attains this name.
That thousandth ray of the sun which has resorted to the moon,
that too reaches Tvaṣṭṛ, Agni, and the supreme honey, both here and beyond.
Then Brahmā, being well-pleased, bestowed it upon his son Atharvan;
and by means of that [knowledge], he became a rishi even more radiant than Brahmā himself.
Indra restrained that seer, saying: "Do not speak thus regarding this honey;
for I do not release anyone alive into this honey before they have first tasted it. (19)
The two divine Aśvins requested honey from that Ṛṣi while he was speaking;
and he then related to them what the Lord of Śacī had said.
The two Nāsatyas said to him:
"May you cause us to drink the honey-liquor quickly with the head of Aśva; then even Indra shall not slay you. (21)
When Dadhyañc spoke those words with the head of a horse for the sake of the Aśvins,
Indra struck off that head of his and deposited it elsewhere.
And the horse-head of Dadhīca, having been struck by the thunderbolt-wielder with his vajra, fell into the middle of the lake on Mount Śaryaṇāvat. || 23 ||
Having arisen from those waters and bestowed various boons upon the living beings until the end of the age, he submerged once again into those very waters.
And Tvaṣṭṛ, the transformer of forms, who is praised with a particle in the middle group [of deities], has no hymn dedicated to him. (25)
That which they call the "lord of the forest" (vanaspati) is this very Agni who is the vanaspati;
for he is the lord of the forests, or rather, he is the protector because he protects them.
With the third verse of the six-verse hymn beginning with "Agnir gṛtsamadena" and "Ayaṃ vanaspatiḥ," [one should worship] him who is praised as "Mandasva. (27)
The praise of him that arises incidentally, both like the sacrificial post and like the tree, is performed with the entire hymn in the third maṇḍala. 28.
There have been many views among the learned regarding the utterances of "svāhā";
however, the settled conclusion is that all of those are indeed this very fire. (29)
For he is the creator of the *svāhā* offerings; here, he alone is the source of their creation. He is the progenitor of all beings, and he is the imperishable one. (30)
The *tanūnapāt* [verse] and that which contains *narāśaṃsa* should both be employed together in all three [sacrifices] that possess both [characteristics]. || 31 ||
Or the second [verse] should be one containing the word *narāśaṃsa* for those desiring progeny; likewise, it should be so for one who desires strength, food, or even prosperity. (32)
The hymn addressed to Agni which is here called the Vaiśvadeva is characterized by universal marks; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is prescribed for recitation among the Vaiśvadeva offerings. (33)
"O Indra, drink this Soma"—this twelvefold seasonal hymn;
in it, he praises seven deities with each verse, together with the season. || 34 ||
In that context, the word "with the seasons" (*ṛtunā*) occurs in six verses;
in four of them it is used together with the plural "seasons" (*ṛtubhiḥ*), while in two others it is used as "with the season" (*ṛtunā*), thus being characterized by both plurality and singularity.
The seasons are praised here by means of deities and particles;
likewise in the Ṛtupraiṣa hymn and also in the Gārtsamada hymn.
But primarily he praised Indra with the first [verse], the Maruts with the second, Tvaṣṭṛ with the third, and Agni with the fourth. (37)
With the fifth [verse], however, one worships Śakra; with the sixth, Devāvṛt and Āvṛdha;
with the first four of the seventh [section], Agni; and with the [next] four, Draviṇodas.
The deity of the Ṛg-mantras is to be known from the direct injunction (ādeśa), not from their indicative mark (liṅga);
for it is not possible to know the deity of these [mantras] in its true nature through their indicative mark alone. (39)
On the eleventh day [he praised] the two Aśvins, and on the twelfth day, this Agni;
Rathītara recited this hymn with separate praises for each.

When each individual deity is praised— whether in a hymn dedicated to many deities, to two deities, or by means of qualities born of their respective actions— that they know as *vibhaktastuti* (separate praise).
The Vaiśvadeva hymns are indeed of three kinds:
those joined with praise of the Sun, those containing universal characteristics (viśvaliṅga), and those consisting of individual praise.
One should know that what is called "separate praise" (pṛthakstuti) involves many deities;
however, that which possesses universal characteristics (viśvaliṅga) is that wherein [the deity is praised] by means of one's own various qualities born of action. (43)
When one praises Sūrya in many ways while addressing all the gods, they say that he praises the gods themselves; that is what is called the "Praise of Sūrya."
But it does not apply to a portion at the beginning of a hymn (*sūkta*) or when [the word] is attached to *auṣasa* or similar terms;
nor does it apply to *sāvitra* with *hrayāmi*, nor to *sūryā* in a sacrifice (*kratu*) or ritual (*makha*). (45)
Nor indeed is this [the case] in such proclamations, in mantras, or in any others;
nor where there might be the word *sajoṣā* or *sajuḥ*. (46)
Even when it is mentioned incidentally, the elder Lāmakāyana has declared that it is indeed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, for it involves the recitation of many [deities]. || 47 ||
Whether it be an unfamiliar or a familiar deity designated anywhere, the sages worship that with mantras; one who knows the scriptures should understand this.
For at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, as well as in their various distinct parts,
ritual acts are sometimes not explicitly prescribed by the agents, yet they are prescribed in some instances.
Action itself is praised in the *sāvitrī* *nivid* by means of action:
that a cow, or two oxen for hauling, or even a swift mare, yields milk. (50)
In the section [of the Vaiśvadeva], he praises Agni and the others, as well as Mitra and the rest, in the praise of the horse; and in this Vaiśvadeva hymn, with the words "yadaibhiḥ," he honors Agni.

Regarding this, they say: "In most cases, while praising one ṛc at the beginning and at the end, one praises another deity as well, either because of a formal connection (pratiyoga) or by way of contextual association (prasaṅga). (52)
That [vowel] in which one pronounces the *arthavāda*s should be known as a *sūktabhāginī*;
but that which one praises incidentally should be known as a *nipātinī*. (53)
In that hymn, she is said to be the recipient of the *saktu* offering in four ways; for in it, the seer praises all the royal seers or even the [ordinary] seers. (54)
Medhātithi, Agastya, Bṛhaduktha, Manu, Gaya, Ṛjiśvan, Vasukarṇa, Śāryāta, Gotama, and Luśa. (55)
Svastyātreya, Parucchepa, Kakṣīvat, Gāthin, Aurva, Nābhāka, and Duvasyu, the son of Mamata, are thus specified. || 56 ||
Vihavya, the sage Kaśyapa, and he who is named Avatsāra; Vāmadeva, Madhucchandas, Pārtha, Dakṣa, and Aditi. || 57 ||
Juhū, the seer Gṛtsamada, the gods, and those who are the seven seers;
Yama, Agni, Tāpasa, Kutsa, Kusīdin, and Trita as well. (58)
And the four brothers, Bandhu and the others, were each separate:
Viṣṇu, Nejamēṣa, and he who was named Saṃvanana. (59)
But all these [gods], with their own various qualities born of their respective actions— both collectively and individually— praised him in separate hymns.
The terrestrial fire, who was previously mentioned as the giver of wealth (draviṇoda), some call Indra because of his status as the giver of strength and riches. (61)
For this Agni is the giver of wealth; he is indeed the bestower of strength.
He is born through strength, and he is churned by the sages during the sacrifice.
They say that sacrificial offerings are wealth when they arise from the oblation;
the priests are the givers of those [offerings], and therefore He Himself is the Giver of Wealth (Draviṇodas).
"He is seen as the son of the Ṛṣis, O youthful one born of strength; or because he was born from the intermediate [region], or because he belongs to the Draviṇodas. (64)
This Agni himself is Draviṇoda; therefore he is called Draviṇodas.
Indeed, the designations of Draviṇodas are seen only in the hymns addressed to Agni. (65)
In this [hymn], of the group of nine dedicated to Indra, that which is the last is dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa;
following that, Brahmaṇaspati is praised in the verse beginning with "somānam. (66)
With the first five *ṛc*s, [the verses] for Sadasaspati and Narāśaṃsa are formed; with the final *carca*, however, Soma and Indra are introduced. (67)
On the fourth [day] Soma and Indra, and on the fifth Dakṣiṇā is predominant;
these connections between the locations and the worlds were mentioned by the Ṛṣi as an incidental discussion.
"Prājāpatya" and likewise "Indra"—these are his two names mentioned here;
there are six others as well, and among them, the first is Prajāpati. || 69 ||
I shall hereafter declare those names which remain: Satpati, Ka, Kāma, and Sadasaspati. (70)
Ilaspati, Vācaspati, and then Brahmaṇaspati;
these are the first and the fifth [verses] of the third hymn at its conclusion.
With the other four [verses], however, this [deity] is neither well-uttered nor does the Ṛc reach him;
but for all the deities, including Prajāpati, all [the verses] indeed [apply]. (72)
Desiring to see perfect devotion, they speak these names;
however, they say that this cannot be so, for this [recitation] is traditionally held to consist of eight [syllables]. (73)
By those very [Maruts] are his sacrifices and oblations fashioned;
this terrestrial Agni is indeed accompanied by the Maruts who occupy the middle station.
In this hymn, [the deity] is praised with the verse beginning "prati tyam";

One might consider that fire to be merely intermediate, and not the terrestrial kind;

May the milch-cow be for you a yielder of milk, the draft-ox a bearer of burdens, and the swift steed a winner by its intelligence;

O Agni, by means of these hymns which are mostly well-composed, the deities therein are to be discerned;

The hymn beginning with "navakaṃ jātavedasyaṃ nan cid yattu vayā" is dedicated to Vaiśvānara; the subsequent one, beginning with "vahnim," is dedicated to Agni. || 117 ||

rose up and begot ṛṣis headed by Kakṣīvat.

he spoke thus of that meat, of the broth, of the sacrificial porridges, and likewise of the oblation.

In this [section], the mention of the garment and the upper garment is proclaimed; likewise, the mention of the victim to be slaughtered, the description of the body, the sacrificial stake, the pillars, and the axe;
the mention of the goat, and the praise of Indra and Pūṣan together.
The hymn known as the Āśvāmīya is said to belong to the Viśvedevas. || 31 ||
Therein are various declarations and the praise of the gods; in this hymn, the verse speaks in indirect terms. O brothers, I shall now describe the three [deities]. 32.
Agni is the beloved, the grey-haired one; Vāyu is the middle brother;
the third here is Ghṛtapṛṣṭha; indeed, seven rays are praised [therein]. (33)
Others say that Agni protects both by raining and by shining,
as he revolves through days and nights, days, months, and seasons.
In five ways, in three ways, in six ways, and indeed in twelve ways, the seer describes the year as revolving like a wheel by means of higher [perceptions]. || 35 ||
He also [beheld] the knowledge of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Cow, Gaurī, Vāc Sarasvatī,
Dharma belonging to the former age, and likewise the Sādhyas, the hosts of gods.
And he [perceived] the various activities of Agni, Vāyu, and Vivasvat,
as well as the sovereign power of Agni and Vāyu over all that is moving and stationary in the world.
The taking up [of water] by means of rays, its release once again,
and the recitation of the deeds of Parjanya, Agni, and Vivasvat are described here.
Mother and son are speech and breath; speech is the mother and the other, breath, is the son.
They call Sarasvant breath and Sarasvatī speech.
The body, joined with the senses, is designated as the "field" (kṣetra).
He who knows it—namely, the vital breath (prāṇa) alone—is therefore called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
The cloud is his chariot, smoke is his [smoke], and water is indeed his garment.
Soma is his bull, and the three purifiers are his sovereign lords. || 41 ||
The *gaurī* [verse] belongs to the *vaiśvadeva*; there should be a separate praise (*pṛthakstuti*) for the subsequent one.
"Indraṃ mitraṃ" and "ime" are addressed to Sūrya; or the last [verse] may belong to Sarasvat. (42)
This *Sūktamala*, however, is a short hymn; it praises knowledge alone, and because of its abundance of expositions, it is therefore called "Salila" (the Flood).
The dialogue between Māruta and Indra is remembered as the supreme *kaya*;
the verses for the Maruts are in odd-numbered meters, while those for Indra are all in even-numbered meters, including the final one.
The first [verse] is in the *ekādaśī* meter, and the subsequent triplet belongs to the Maruts.
However, in that context, agency is stated to belong to the triplet of verses alone, and not to the other.
This history, concerning events of the past, is proclaimed by the seers:
while Śatakratu was traveling through the sky, he encountered the Maruts.
Having seen them, Indra praised them, and those sages spoke to Indra;
Agastya, through his ascetic power, knew their conversation in its true essence.
Having prepared the oblation for Indra, he quickly approached them and praised the Maruts with the three hymns beginning with the words "tan-nu."
With the verse "mahaścit" and with "sahasram," he desires to give that offered oblation, intended for Indra, to the Maruts.
Having understood and discerned his state of being, Indra said to him, "No.
For there is nothing of tomorrow nor of today; who knows that which is wonderful? (50)
"Upon the shifting of someone's wealth, their very mind perishes.
"Why not? Indra asked. Agastya replied, "Your brothers. (51)
"Consult with the Maruts; do not slay us, O Śatakratu!"—with these words, Indra reproached Mānyu in this [hymn], saying, "Why [do you act thus] toward us, brother? (52)
Agastya pacified the agitated Indra with this hymn;
having performed a conciliatory rite, he offered that sacrificial oblation to those very [gods].
Then Indra made those Maruts drinkers of Soma at the pressing of the juice;
therefore, one should know that the Maruts are praised together with Indra by means of the *nipāta* (vocative particle). 54.
With a joyful soul, the sage praised them individually once more—with two hymns for the Maruts, and six for Indra; but he surpassed them all.
Indra was praised with four verses beginning with "stutāsaḥ";
together with those [verses] and with the Maruts, he became known as Marutvān wherever Indra was present.
When his wife, the illustrious Lopāmudrā, had bathed at the end of her menstrual period,
the sage began to address her in private, desiring sexual union. She, however, spoke with both eyes wide open regarding what she intended to do first.
Then Agastya, desiring to sport with her, gratified her with the next two verses.
Having understood through ascetic power the entire disposition of those two who desired to sport, and having heard their transgression, I, the supreme celibate student, sang this. (59)
Having instructed him and embraced him, the two gurus smelled his head;
smiling, they both said to him, "You are blameless, my son."

Then Agastya praised the Aśvins with five hymns beginning with "yuvo rājāṃsi," and with the following hymn beginning with "katara," he praised Heaven and Earth. Then, with the hymn beginning with "ā no viśvān divaukasaḥ," he praised all the dwellers of heaven.
And [he recites] "pitum annam," "samiddho agniḥ," and "agna āyūṃṣi pavase" and "agne naya. || 6.2 ||
Some know this hymn to be that of Bṛhaspati, which is unassailable, supreme, and secret like a porcupine's quill; others know it as a praise of the waters, the plants, and the sun.
Agastya perceived it as a destroyer of poison, due to his apprehension of poison.
But here, the "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) [portion], which has lost its form, is the leading of the hymn (*sūkta*); however, in this case, it consists of two verses (*dvṛca*). || 64 ||
Gṛtsamada praised Agni Jātavedas with the Āprī hymns;
then Agni, kindled by the sacrifice, [is honored], and therefore I invoke Agni with seven [verses].
Having united his self through austerity, he bears the great body of Indra.
In a mere moment, he was seen in heaven, in the sky, and here on earth.
Thinking him to be Indra, the two Daityas of fearsome prowess,
Dhuni and Cumuri, both armed with weapons, rushed toward him.
Having understood their intention to commit evil,
the sage recited the deeds of Indra with the hymn beginning with "yo jātaḥ."
While those deeds of Indra were being recounted, fear quickly entered them both. Saying, "This is the opportunity," Indra then struck them down.
Having slain those two, Śakra addressed the sage Gṛtsamada:
"Behold me as you wish, O friend; you have become dear to me."
"Accept a boon from me, and let your ascetic power be inexhaustible.
To him who was thus bowed down, the sage replied, "O best among speakers, [grant this] for us. (71)
May there be safety for our bodies, and may our speech be pleasing to the heart;
O Indra, we meditate upon you, that we may be possessed of brave sons and abundant wealth.
"O Indra, we recognize you in birth after birth; this devotion of mine is directed toward you alone. You are not the sinful Rathītara. (73)
"Nirukta, this desirable boon—O Indra, the most excellent ones [of the Vedas]—this entire boon has been chosen by me with the final Ṛc. Having heard this, the Lord of Śacī [Indra] [responded]. (74)
Having said "So be it," Indra grasped his right hand;
and the sage, out of friendship, touched his hand with his own.
Thus, together they proceeded toward the abode of Mahendra.
There, Purandara himself, out of affection, honored him with due respect.
He honored that Ṛṣi with the rites prescribed by rule;
and because of their friendship, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, spoke to him again.
"O best of seers, because you shall gladden us by chanting [the hymns], therefore you shall become known as Gṛtsamada, the son of Śunahotra. (78)
Then, with twelve hymns beginning with "śrudhi," the seer praised Indra;
even as he was offering praise, he beheld Brahmaṇaspati there.
He praised Bṛhaspati with verses that clearly revealed his signs;
and he, in turn, praised him with the four subsequent [verses].
In this [verse] beginning with "gaṇānāṃ viśvam," Indra and Brāhmaṇaspati [are the deities];
or, by association, Bṛhaspati or Brahmaṇaspati alone. || 81 ||
He praised with a single hymn the difference in power between the two [Aśvins] and among Mitra,
Varuṇa, Dakṣa, Bhaga, and Aryaman, who were born from portions of them;
this collection of hymns concerning the Ādityas is called the Vāruṇa-sūkta.
The hymn beginning with "vāruṇī yo me" and so forth is the destroyer of bad dreams and other such evils. ||83||
The hymn *dhṛtavratā* belongs to the Viśvedevas; the next one, beginning with *pra hi kratum*, is addressed to Indra, though in it Indra and Soma are praised together.
In the verse beginning with *sarasvatī tvam*, however, the intermediate Speech (Vāc) is praised in the middle hemistich.
The praise of Bṛhaspati which belongs to us, and that Ṛc of yours which is the praise of the Maruts. ||85||
Our Vaiśvadeva hymn should begin with the verse "asya" (RV 1.142.1);
then follow two verses addressed to Dyāvāpṛthivī and Tvaṣṭṛ, or alternatively, two verses addressed to Indra. ||86||
There are two [verses] each for Rākā and Sinīvālī; likewise, there are six beginning with Guṅgū and ending with the last.
Prior to that are two verses for Kuhū, known as "Kuhūm aham" (I am Kuhū). Following those are two verses for Anumati, known as "Anu naḥ" and "Anvid".
May Dhātṛ, the first among the four deities, grant us wealth. || 88 ||
Then, seeing a fierce deer on his left, the sage himself approached, trembling with fear, [reciting] "praramā te dhārāvarā" (the most excellent showers for you). || 89 ||
With the verse "Praise the renowned one," he praised that very deity in this hymn, seeking to propitiate him;
thereafter, in the subsequent verses of the hymn, the deity was praised as "Aponapāt. (90)
The hymn beginning with "tubhyam" is for the Ṛtu sacrifice; following the Sāvitra [hymns] is the Āśvina [hymn];
and Soma, Pūṣan, and Aditi are praised in the Somapauṣṇa [sacrifice] by means of the final verse.
In the northwest is the verse for Indra and Vāyu; then follow five *prauga* triplets (*ṛc*).
With the words "pretya," he praises the two *havirdhāna* sheds; there, the word "agni" occurs as a secondary insertion (*nipāta*).
Then follow the verses for Heaven and Earth beginning with "dyauḥ"; these are in the *havirdhāna* sheds. || 92 ||

Desiring once more to receive praise, Indra became a kapiñjala partridge and, assuming the form of a bird, cried out as the rishi was about to depart for the south in accordance with his wish. Seeing him in the form of a bird with the divine eye of a seer, [the rishi spoke].
But Kanikrada praised him with two hymns from the latter portion [of the Ṛgveda]. || 94 ||
He who, having ruled the earth, attained the status of a Brahmarṣi through austerity and begot one hundred and one sons—
he, the son of Gathi, recited the Sūkta of Soma, as well as the Āgneya hymns and those that follow.

In the hymn to Vaiśvānara, there are two verses beginning with "samidhā" addressed to Agni; the two following hymns here are addressed to Heaven and Earth, Dawn, the Nipātas, the Waters, and then the Gods and the Fathers, as well as Mitra. || 96 ||
In the hymns dedicated to Agni, Vaiśvānara, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas are indeed seen being praised;
wherever there is praise for one, there one should recognize that it applies to all, whether explicitly praised or not, as well as the implied meanings and the sense of comparison. (97)

The royal sages Gṛtsamadas, Vasiṣṭhas, Bharadvājas, Kuśikas, and Gotamas; all the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Aṅgirases, the Atris, Aditi, the Bhojas, the Kaṇvas, the Bhṛgus, the two worlds, and the quarters. || 98 ||

In hymns dedicated to Savitṛ, Soma, the Aśvins, and the Maruts; in those to Indra-Agni, Rudra, Sūrya, and Uṣas—the deities who receive their share of the hymn do not cause harm when they are praised at the beginning, the end, or interspersed within the middle. (99)

The seventeenth chapter belongs to Agni; [it begins with] "ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye. These two verses belong to Kaṇva; [then follow] two addressed to the sacrificial post, and five [verses] beginning with "añjanti. || 100 ||
The remaining verses are for many sacrificial posts; the eighth verse, however, belongs to the Viśvedevas.
Its final portion is declared to be for the wood-cutting tool, while the sixth is said to be for Indra and Agni.
One should recite the verse beginning with "agnim uṣasam vaiśvadevam," as well as "dadhikrām";
then the verse "agne indraścarṣaṇiḥ" addressed to Agni-Indra, and the triplet beginning with "vaiśvānaraḥ. (102)
Let the Marut-host go forth with its hundred streams; the heavy hymn of praise goes forth.
Your strengths, O Vājins, laud the seasons; the priest lauds them as he churns. 103.
With the verse "puroṣyāsaḥ," he praises the fires on the hearths (dhiṣṇya);
and there, they are to be known as both the Hotṛ and the divine ones.
Twenty-three [verses] beginning with "icchanti" belong to Indra;
thereafter, the hymn beginning with "pra" and the verses concerning the rivers were uttered by Viśvāmitra. (105)
Acting as the domestic priest for the sake of performing sacrifices together with Sudās, the Ṛṣi Śamīka spoke of the confluence of the Vipāś and Śutudrī rivers. || 106 ||
There, proclamations are seen expressed in the dual, the plural, and the singular;
they are recited by hemistichs, by half-verses, or by quarter-verses, and even in rivers they are uttered in the singular.
In the first two verses and a half, the words of Viśvāmitra were heard;
by these *ṛg* verses, the rivers spoke to the *ṛṣi* using the plural form. (108)
The other two deities who were proclaimed by the Sage in the sixth, eighth, fourth, and tenth [verses], as well as in the seventh and sixth *ṛc*s— || 109 ||
Those two [verses] are to be known as "nipātinau" (falling ones) in the final verse of the Aindrāpārvatī hymn;
they create what is called a "putrikā," just like a daughter. One pours semen into her, and that is proclaimed as "tacchāsa. (110)
The giving of an inheritance to a daughter is prohibited by the verse beginning with "no" (na).
Furthermore, he [the author] mentions her younger brother as being like a son of the elder brother,
as in the case of Śakti giving [wealth] to the son of Gāthin at the great sacrifice of Sudās.
His mind, forcibly restrained, became despondent and lost its senses;
for him, the Jamadagnis brought from the abode of the Sun and bestowed that speech known as Sārparājñī, which belongs to Brahmā or to the Sun. || 113 ||
Then that voice of the Kuśikas dispelled that delusion.
And while he was in that state, Viśvāmitra enlightened him regarding all the Kuśikas;
having regained his speech, he, with a joyful soul, honored those sages,
praising speech itself with two verses beginning with "sasarparīḥ."
One should say "sthirau" (be firm) when stepping over the limbs of a draft animal or the ox itself while going toward the house.
Then, proceeding toward his home with his own body,
he seized the four others who were known there as the haters of Vasiṣṭha.
These were proclaimed by Viśvāmitra and are known as "curses" (abhiśāpa);
they are spoken out of hatred for enemies and are indeed spells of malevolent magic (abhicārika). || 118 ||
O Vasiṣṭhas, they do not listen to that which is approved by the Teacher;
from either reciting it or even listening to it, a great fault arises.
Their heads split into a hundred pieces by its being recited or heard;
their children die, therefore one should not recite them.
The seer praised all the gods with four verses beginning with "imaṃ"; he lauded them as the supreme state, regarding them all as the universal self. 121.
Declaring that the asura-nature of the gods is that one Great One (mahat), [I call upon] the Aśvins, Mitra, and the Ṛbhus; O Dhenu, Mitra, come hither, come hither to you! 1.22.
The [verse] beginning with "vaiśvadevī" is to be known as addressed to Mitra; there are five [verses] for Mitra.
Here, the triplet beginning with "aindrārbhava" is the final one in the Ārbhava hymn.

In the first two *ṛcas*, Indra is the deity; from the fifth [verse] onwards, there are six subsequent triplets (*tṛcas*) dedicated to Uṣas, each with a different deity. The first [of these] is addressed to Indra and Varuṇa, and the next is addressed to Bṛhaspati. (124)
Jamadagni praised Pauṣṇa, Sāvitra, Saumya, and Maitrāvaruṇa as the last; by that, he gratified the two gods who increase the rite (devāvṛtāvṛdhau).
For the sake of worshipping the gods, sages, and ancestors, he gave the entrails of the sinners to the dogs;
indeed, it was he who, in the form of a hawk, brought the honey for the slayer of Vṛtra.
With fifteen verses he praised Agni, and with sixteen subsequent ones, "Ṛṣis tvām," the sage Gautama extolled Indra. Thus did Gautama proceed.

In these three verses, "sa" (he), "bhrātaram" (brother), and "tvā" (you) are the words that function as *nipātas*; others say that "agniḥ" (Agni) is the *nipāta* used for praise in connection with Varuṇa. 128.
In the hymn whose deity is indicated by its internal marks, some maintain that Agni alone is the seer;
however, with the two verses beginning "Bodha," he praises Soma alone.
And for the sake of that very life-span, the two Aśvins were praised by the two others; [the latter] spoke even while still in the womb: "I shall not be born in the ordinary way. (130)
Aditi, seeking her own welfare, instructed her son Indra;
as soon as he was born, he summoned the sage Vāmadeva for battle.
Then Vāmadeva, while milking the cow, likewise placed his own strength within him.
He conquered him by his might for ten days and ten nights.
While selling him in the assembly of sages with the words "Who is this?", Gautama himself praised him with the hymn beginning, "None indeed [is like] Indra. (132)
With the verse beginning "kimādutāsī," he cast away half of her wrath;
then the Ṛṣi [took] those forms, powers, and acts of fortitude belonging to him.
And likewise, various deeds were recounted for the sake of Aditi;
indeed, the self-praise in the triplet beginning with "I am" was like a hymn of praise unto him.
The hymn beginning with "pra su" is a praise of the falcon (śyena) in nine verses;
however, the five-verse hymn beginning with "parābhiḥ" praises Indra together with Soma. || 136 ||
Krauṣṭuki, however, considers this hymn to be primarily concerned with Soma;
he regards it as a praise of Indra through these three verses beginning with "divaścit. (1.37)
The teacher Śākaṭāyana considered Uṣas to be the middle [deity];
moreover, those praised in the Ṛgveda here are Vāma, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Aryaman.
"He is called Pūṣan because he nourishes (karūlati)," according to the Vedic revelation;
