"he praises our supreme Sun," so says Āśvalāyana. (13.9)
For Indra’s horses are the bay steeds; Agni’s horses are the ruddy ones;
Sūrya’s are the tawny steeds, and Vāyu’s are indeed the Niyuts.
The donkey was assigned to the Aśvins, the goats to Pūṣan, the swift horses to the Maruts, and the dappled red cows to the Uṣas. (141)
The dark bay horses of Savitṛ, the swift ones, and those of all forms belonging to Bṛhaspati—
these are praised together with their deities, though in some cases they are praised in fewer numbers.
Whosoever is seen here in praise, along with his lifespan and his vehicle, one should know him alone as the praised; for he is indeed that Self in many forms.
The word *kanīnakā* refers to what remains after the [previous] statement; here, the praise of the two bay horses (*haryoḥ*) is being expressed.
Furthermore, the four syllables following this should be understood as *ū* and *apragṛhya* in the *vidradha* [meter]. 144.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Bṛhaddevatā.
The *preti* verses consist of five; the *ārbhava* consists of three; and beyond these are the *dādhikra* verses.
Among the *dādhikra* verses, that which stands at the beginning praises Heaven and Earth (*ṛgdyāvāpṛthivyau*).
The three— Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya— were praised by him with words and names out of his sight, using the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
The hymn dedicated to Sūrya beginning with "haṃsa" is prescribed in the Aitareyaka;
two hymns are dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa, and after those, three are dedicated to the Aśvins—what [is there beyond]? (3)
The seven verses beginning with "agraṃ vāyo vihī" are proclaimed as dedicated to Vāyu;
those dedicated to Indra and Vāyu are nine; and those dedicated to Indra alone are three hundred and six.

This pair of verses (dvṛca), which has the aforementioned deities and is the best for paralyzing [the enemy], is a hymn of praise to Indra and Bṛhaspati; these eight verses are traditionally remembered as such. ||5||
Some say that this hymn belongs to Bṛhaspati, others to Uṣas; the praise of the priest's office is expressed in the triplet beginning with "sa indra. (6)
Of those, two are addressed to Savitṛ; one is addressed to the Viśvedevas; "mahī dyāvāpṛthivīya" is the next;
"kṣetrasya" consists of three verses addressed to Kṣetrapati; "śunaṃ vāhāḥ" is addressed to Śuna, while the subsequent Ṛc is addressed to Śunādevī. || 7 ||
Vāyu is Śunaḥ, and Sūrya is Sīra; thus they call Vāyu and Sūrya "Śunāsīrau.
Yāska, however, considered Śunāsīra to be Indra, while Śākapūṇi considers them to be Sūrya and Indra.
Śunāsīrau are praised in the fifth [verse], while those two [verses] are for Sītā in the sixth and seventh.
The quarter-verse beginning "śunaṃ naḥ phālāḥ" praises agriculture, and "śunaṃ kīnāśāḥ" praises the plowmen, the men who live by farming. (9)
Parjanya is praised in the first foot here; in the third, the seer, desiring wealth, spoke the final [verse].
Or rather, he praises agriculture, for this entire hymn belongs to the middle Agni, originating from the ocean. (10)

Whether it is addressed to Āditya as declared by the Brāhmaṇas, or seen as addressed to Agni through the Ājya-sūkta, or a hymn of praise to the waters, or a hymn of praise to clarified butter— some say this [sūkta] is dedicated to the cow, while others call it solar.
Having dispelled the darkness seen by Svarbhānu from the sun, Atri praised Agni with twenty-seven hymns, saying, "He has awakened. (12)
Traivṛṣṇa, Trasadasyu, Aśvamedha, and Ṛṇañcaya—these, being praised, should be examined among the Atris here and there. 13.
At night, Tryaruṇa of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the priest Vṛśa Jāna, mounted the chariot belonging to Traivṛṣṇa and grasped the reins of the horses.
As the Brahmin youth’s chariot was passing, it cut off his head;
and the king said to that priest, "You are a sinner. (15)
Having seen the Atharva-Aṅgirasa mantras and having restored that child to life, he abandoned the king out of anger and took refuge in another country. ||16||
Because that sage had departed, Hara did not consume even the fire;
for due to his absence, no sacrificial offerings placed in the fire were ever cooked. ||17||
Then the king, deeply distressed, approached him and propitiated him; having understood that great sage's intention, he placed him once again at the forefront [of his ministers]. (18)
In that royal palace, he, being pleased, searched for the fire-stick (araṇi) of Dhara;
and he found that wife of the king to be a piśācī.
Seated together with her upon a couch and even upon a rug, he addressed her with a Ṛgvedic verse, asking, "Who is this man for you? (Ṛgveda 10.10.4).
Hara, assuming the form of a youth, addressed her;
and as soon as she was told, "O Vijyotis," Agni suddenly blazed forth.
Enduring her approach and illuminating the surroundings,
he consumed that Piśācī wherever she sat down.
Thus indeed has this Dvṛca been explained in the Bhāllavi Brāhmaṇa;
such is the traditional teaching (śruti) in the work known as the Nidāna regarding the Chandogas.
This reflection might indeed arise in consideration of this well-spoken verse:
"For external mantras come into being when impelled by what is seen in the injunctions. (24)
Mantras are seen indicated in a single portion of the Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, the Jāmadagnya and the Stokīya mantras appear in the Aitareyaka.

The fifth hymn here is the *Āprī* for the well-kindled fire; in this [section], the final verse is addressed to the Viśvedevas, while the penultimate one is addressed to Indra and Agni. There are twelve verses addressed to Indra, and Uśanas is praised therein.
Indeed, he was bound by the foot with the words "uśanā" and by the dwarf [Vāmana].
In this [hymn] beginning with "indrākutsa," Indra was praised together with Kutsa;
and in the five verses beginning with "yattvā sūrya," the deed of Atri is celebrated. (28)
In this hymn beginning with "anasvanta," some say that the seer Atri himself, gratified by their gift, praised these royal sages. (29)
From them, he received both blessings and requests,
and [he offered] a gift toward the fire consisting of ten thousand cows, three hundred, and twenty more.
King Tryaruṇa gave a golden chariot drawn by two cows to Atri;
Trasadasyu gave a hundred horse-sacrifices and much wealth in cattle.
Some say that he spoke that hymn to the king;
for the seer would not have given himself to himself, yet he did accept it from the monarch.
Ṛṇañcaya [appointed] Babhru, the son of Atri, as the seer for the office of officiating priest.
At the Soma sacrifice where a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā was given, he chose him as his priest; and he, too, performed the sacrifice for him.
And King Rāma gave him hundreds and thousands [of gold pieces],
as well as four great heroes and four golden [ornaments].
During the Pravargya rites, his Mahāvīra vessels were made of gold;
having accepted them, the sage was traveling on the road by way of the middle fire.
Questioned by Indra, he explained that auspicious [sacrifice] with four verses;
and who indeed among you two would offer eleven Vaiśvadeva oblations beyond this? (36)
The ten *māruta* hymns are praised with the *ṛc* beginning "pra," while Śaunaka has stated that Savitṛ is praised with the third *ṛc* beginning "ud. (37)

The triplet beginning with "upeti" belongs to Bṛhaspati; the next verse belongs to the Maruts; the verse beginning with "tamu ṣṭuhi" belongs to Rudra; and the verse beginning with "pra suṣṭutiḥ" likewise [belongs to him]. (38)
The deities were invoked in many ways by teachers such as Śaunaka and others;
Śākapūṇi [identified them with] Ilaspati, while Gālava [identified them with] Parjanya and Agni.
Yāska, however, considered Pūṣan to be praised; Śaunaka, on the other hand, [considered] Indra;
Bhāguri, Vaiśvānara; and this [hymn] belongs to the Maruts and the Aśvins.
The verses for the Adhvaryus belong to Vāyu, those for the Daśa-patra to Soma, and the subsequent one to Indra;
furthermore, they drive Agni toward the Dharma, while the Ṛc praises the Aśvins—go forth! 41.
In the first half-verse, Agni is mentioned here along with Pūṣan and Vāyu;
then, in the second [half-verse], the gods dwelling in heaven are praised as they arrive. ||42||
He praises the intermediate Speech; thereafter he praises Bṛhaspati as the elder, and Āditya with the words "pra vaḥ"; here Vāyu is spoken of.
Regarding the verse "As of old," Kauṣītaki himself has stated that it belongs either to Soma or to Indra among the gods, or it is a hidden Vaiśvadeva hymn dedicated to Prajāpati. 44.

Among those, the third is said to be "I invoke the gods" (devān huve), which is supreme; however, the wives of the gods (devapatnyaḥ) are praised in the two-verse hymn beginning with "the wives of the gods" (devānām patnīḥ). 45.
And this [hymn] belongs to four deities; Indra and Vāyu are praised with three [verses]: "O Vāyu, come hither" (vāyav ā yāhi) and "To Vāyu" (vāyum).
Rodasī is praised here with one verse: "The chariot... (rathaṃ vaḥ). The Maruts are praised in the verse belonging to Rudra’s consort: "Whose... (yasyāḥ). ||46||
In this [hymn], "ā rudrāsaḥ," the host of Rudras is praised;
however, it is traditionally held that the name of the host of Maruts is "rudrāḥ. (47)
Both this fire and that one are terrestrial and intermediate fires;
in the verse beginning "O Agni, with the Maruts," they are praised together with the Maruts.
All women are the intermediate speech; every man is the intermediate [speech];
and all the Maruts are the intermediate [speech], though they are distinct from one another due to their differences in qualities. 49.
There was a royal sage, the son of Darbha, known as Rathavīti.

Desiring to perform a sacrifice, that king approached Atri and, having propitiated him, stood with palms joined in reverence, announcing himself, his purpose, and his need. (Drahyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra 5.61)
He chose the seer Mātreya Ārchanānasa for the office of officiating priest.
Accompanied by his son, Śyāvaśva—the son indeed of Arcanānas, who was himself the son of Atri’s son—approached that king for the successful completion of the sacrifice. ||52||
Then Arcanāna, together with his son, having gone to the king, performed a sacrifice for him; he who had joyfully been taught all the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs by his father.
And while the sacrifice was being performed, he beheld the illustrious princess;
the thought arose in his mind, "May this princess become my daughter-in-law. (54)
At that time, the mind of Śyāvāśva was indeed attached to her;
he said to his patron, "O King, unite with me. ||55||
Desiring to give his daughter to Śyāvāśva, the king said to his queen: "What is your opinion? Shall I indeed give my daughter to Śyāvāśva? (56)
"Indeed, the son of Atri is not weak;
he is our son-in-law," she said to the king, "for I am born of a lineage of royal sages. (5)
"A son-in-law who is not a seer (ṛṣi) cannot [be our husband], for he has not seen the mantras.
Let the maiden be given to a seer; thus she will become the mother of the Veda.
For a seer considers himself the father of the Veda by virtue of being its seer of the mantras. (58)
Having consulted with his wife, the king rejected him, saying,
"No one who is not a seer can truly be a son-in-law."
When the sacrifice was completed, the sage, having been rejected by him, turned back;
however, the mind of Śyāvāśva’s daughter did not turn back at all.
Then those two returned together and approached both Śaśīyasī and the king Taranta Purumīḷha.
Tarantapuru and Mīḍha were two kings who were descendants of Vaidadaśvi;
those two monarchs themselves paid honor to those two sages.
The king showed him to the queen and her son, Taranta;
and with Anumati’s approval, she bestowed upon him various kinds of wealth.
Having gone to Śyāvāśva— who was honored by his patrons with a great abundance of goats, sheep, cattle, and horses— and having paid homage to Atri, the father and son returned to their own hermitage.
They both paid homage to the great seer Atri, who was blazing with splendor.
Śyāvāśva thought to himself, "Because I have not seen the mantra, I [am at fault]. (65)
Alas, I have not obtained a maiden beautiful in all her limbs;
even if I were to become a seer of mantras, my joy would be great.
As he was thus reflecting in the forest, a host of Maruts appeared;
he saw them standing at his side, appearing as if they were identical in form to himself.
And seeing those Maruts, who were of equal age, with golden ornaments upon their chests— those gods of human form who were all of the same age— [he was struck with wonder].
Śyāvāśva, filled with wonder, then asked, "Who are these? and they replied, "The Maruts.
Thereupon, the Maruts recognized them as the gods who are the sons of Rudra.
Having recognized them with these verses beginning with "ya īṃ vahanti," he praised them accordingly;
for the seer considered that transgression of his own to be immense.
That he did not praise [him] immediately upon seeing him, and that he asked "Who are you?", [caused them concern];
yet, being thus praised with a hymn and pleased, the sons of Pṛśni departed.
Having unfastened the golden ornament from their own garments, they then gave it to him;
and when the Maruts had departed, the highly illustrious Śyāvāśva [remained].
Then he went to the daughter of Rathavīti with his mind;
that seer, intending to bestow himself immediately upon Rathavīti, [proceeded].
Having perceived Rathavīti with his divine vision, he appointed Rātri as his messenger using these two verses beginning with "etaṃ me stomam. (74)
"Upon the beautiful ridge of the Himavat, he dwells," he said,
having understood the command of the sage and being urged by the goddess Rātri.
Taking that maiden, the son of Dṛbhya approached Arcanānas;
having clasped his feet and standing before him with humility and palms joined in reverence. || 76 ||
"I am Rathaviti, the son of Darbha," he declared his name;
"and as for what I previously rejected you when you desired union with me."
Therefore, forgive me; let there be salutation to you, and do not be angry with me, O Blessed One.
You are the son of a seer, yourself a seer, and the father of the seer, O Blessed One.
"Come, please accept this daughter-in-law," the king himself said,
having honored her with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and the honey-mixture.
Having given a hundred white horses, he permitted Śaśīyasī, Taranta, and the king Purumīḷha to return to their homes.
Having praised with the hymn beginning "ṣaḍbhiḥ sanat," the seer also went to his abode;
there are eleven subsequent [hymns] dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa according to the Ṛta.
Six *aśvinī* [days] are for the sake of conception; the praise of the *pañcarca-upaniṣad* is performed seven times; and having committed other offenses, marriage becomes fruitless. (82)
According to the sacred tradition, he was indeed made a Ṛṣi by means of the Aśvamedha sacrifice performed by Bhārata;
yet, upon his eighth offense, that king was confined in a wooden trough.
Having cast it into the *ṛbhu* fire, he preserved what had spilled during the night;
the seer then gratified the two Aśvins, the lords of beauty (*śubhaspatī*), with the hymn beginning "O Aśvins" (*so 'śvināv iti*). (84)
Having extracted him from that state, those two made him fruitful once again;
for the sake of his own internal essence, he was like the embryo within him as he slept.
Or, as in the case of the known [rite] beginning with "yathā vāta," the other two verses are used for Aśvinī;
that consecration is seen to be effective even for embryos that are miscarried. || 86 ||
The occurrence of the state of being would likewise be of such a nature, for it is indeed seen as such;
for this very form is seen through the terms "jarāyu" and "garbha. || 87 ||
In the great hymn to Uṣas and Savitṛ, [the gods] yoke [their chariots];
indeed, Parjanya is praised as "bali" (the powerful one), and in this [hymn], the middle earth is praised. ||88||
"O God Savitṛ, today for us this [hymn] is the destroyer of bad dreams;
next, one addressed to Varuṇa for the Sovereign (Samrāj); and the following two are addressed to Indra-Agni. (89)
The supreme limb of Viṣṇu is the excellent hymn (sūkta) dedicated to the Maruts called Evayāmarut; the hymn beginning with "dyoḥ" is dedicated to Indra. 90.

The Śrīsūkta is a benediction for those who possess the fortune of sons; the following six [verses] are likewise [benedictory]. Or rather, that [sūkta] is the remover of misfortune for Lakṣmī, and Agni is the deity presiding over it. 91.

In the rite for the embryo, [the verses] "Possessing offspring" and "O you two whose sons are living" are recited; [the verses] "Of various forms" and "The milk-yielding ones flow together" are likewise recited. (92)
In blessings, designations, and ritual procedures, the deity resides in the indeclinables;
here, the knower of mantras should examine [the deity] through gender and syntactical context. 93.
Between the application of a mantra and the mantra itself, the application is more powerful;
there should be an examination of these two according to the rule, for mantras are merely expressive. ||94||
Therefore, there is no contradiction with those [mantras];
rather, the words contained within them that denote qualities are indeed terms of conventional understanding. ||95||
When mantras are subordinate and ritual acts are primary, it is understood that the deities are both primary and subordinate. (96)
Desirous of offspring, Prajāpati performed a sacrificial session lasting three years, together with the Sādhyas and all the gods. || 97 ||
There, at the initiation of speech, she arrived in embodied form;
seeing her there simultaneously, both Ka and Varuṇa were struck with wonder.
The semen spilled; Vāyu cast it into the fire by chance. From the flames Bhṛgu was born, and from the embers the seer Aṅgiras.
Having seen the two sons of Prajāpati, Speech (Vāk) spoke:
"May a third seer also become my son right here, along with these two. (100)
Having been told "So be it," Prajāpati replied with these words.
From him was born the seer Atri, possessing a splendor equal to the sun and fire.
The sage who was born from the embers had a son, Bṛhaspati;
Bharadvāja, who is called Vidathin, was the son of Bṛhaspati. || 102 ||
He who was the preceptor among the Maruts was indeed the grandson of Aṅgiras;
this sixth maṇḍala is said to belong to him together with his son.
In that [section], at the beginning, there are thirteen hymns dedicated to Agni starting with "tvaṃ hyagne";
then there are three hymns dedicated to Agni Vaiśvānara, beginning with "mūrdhānaṃ". (104)
In this [section], there are twenty-nine verses beginning with "piba" dedicated to Indra;
after that, in the verse beginning with "agne sa kṣeṣat," two deities are mentioned as being invoked.
The two verses beginning with "protaye" and "nū ma" are remembered as being addressed to the Viśvedevas;
however, the second verse has its final word dedicated to Indra, thus constituting a praise of the cows. (106)
In this verse beginning with "āsasrāṇāsaḥ," both Vāyu and Indra are praised together;
however, Indra is praised here primarily, while Vāyu is present as a subordinate participant.
Some declare this triplet of verses to be dedicated to Soma and Indra;
however, the triplet beginning with "ya ānayad" is traditionally recited as a praise of Bṛbu.
Śaṃyu praises his father in the final pada of the triplet;
the subsequent five-verse hymn beginning with "svāduṣkila ayam" is dedicated to Soma.
In this [passage], Indra is praised as the primary deity, while Soma is mentioned as a subordinate participant;
for it is heard in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa that Indra's drinks are to be followed by those of Indra. (110)
The first quarter praises the gods; the next, the earth;
the third, Bṛhaspati; and the final quarter, Indra alone. (111)
"O Lord of the Forest, firm of limb"—this is what the teachers call the supreme state of being;
there are three *ṛc* verses for the touching of the chariot, and three for the drum, while here follows the praise (*saṃstava*). (112)
The hymn beginning with "samaśvaparṇāḥ" belongs to Agni; the next ten verses belong to Indra; then there is a triplet for Agni by Tṛṇapāṇika;
the following triplet is addressed to the Maruts in the Pṛśni-hymn; and after that, a double verse is addressed to the Viśvedevas, followed again by another.
It should belong either to Āditya or to the Maruts;
there are four verses addressed to Pūṣan beginning with "ā mā pūṣan";
one should know that the subsequent two-verse hymn belongs to the Maruts.
The mention of the last two [verses] belongs to Dyubhvah, or alternatively, to Pr̥śni.
I praise four hymns dedicated to the Viśvedevas; beyond these, the second [verse] is for Agni, the fourth for Vāyu, and the fifth for the Aśvins. 115.
The seventh Ṛc praises Vāc; here, the eighth [praises] Pūṣan;
the ninth [praises] Tvaṣṭṛ; and with the words "of the world" (bhuvanasya), the next two [verses] praise Rudra.
The seer addressed Viṣṇu alone with the hymn beginning "yo rajāṃsi" (which belongs to the Maruts);
and the hymn beginning "abhyandraya" is dedicated to Savitṛ, while others are dedicated to Rudra, Agni, and the Aśvins. 117.

The two verses beginning with "agnīparjanyā" and "anayā sauryau" are dedicated to Agni and Parjanya; the verse beginning with "udu tyat" is dedicated to Aditi; the four verses beginning with "vayaṃ" are dedicated to Pūṣan; and the verse following that is dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan. 118.
Some declare the wearer of matted locks, the best of chariot-warriors, to be Raudra; others say "I shall now proclaim him who belongs to Indra and Agni"; this one here I praise as Sarasvata. 119.
In the two verses beginning with "āśvine" and "coṣase," and in the two verses beginning with "mārutaṃ tu vapūṃṣi" and "upa," he recites the propitiation of the Aśvins. ||120||
The one addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa begins with "viśveṣāṃ vaḥ satām";
that addressed to Indra and Varuṇa begins with "śruṣṭī"; and the last is addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu.
Dyāvāpṛthivī, Savitṛ, Indra and Soma, and Bṛhaspati were each praised with their own respective hymns; those two, Soma and Rudra, were praised together. 122.
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the wife, the earth, the horse, and likewise the elephant—
these are the seven jewels of all universal monarchs.
Abhyāvartin, Āyamāna, and Prastoka Sārñjaya also arrived; having been defeated by Vāraśikha in battle, they came to Bharadvāja.
Having approached him and propitiated him, they announced their names and said:
"O Brahmin, know us to have been utterly defeated in battle by the arrows of Śiva. (125)
"Let us two, as your priests, conquer the base-born Kṣatriyas;
for even that Kṣatriya power must be understood as Brahman, which protects eternally. (126)
The sage, having said "So be it," spoke to his son Pāyu:
"Make these two kings invincible to their enemies."
Having said "So be it" to his father, he consecrated the equipment for battle belonging to those two separately with the hymn beginning with "jīmūtasya."
The first verse of this hymn praises the armored warrior;
the second, however, [praises] the bow, while the third is for the consecration of the bowstring. (129)
The first [verse] praises the chariot, while the fifth praises the quiver;
by half of the sixth [verse], the charioteer is praised, and by the other half, the reins. || 130 ||
The seventh [verse] praises the horses, the eighth the armory, the ninth the chariot-protectors, and the tenth the deities of battle. || 131 ||
The eleventh praises the arrow, the twelfth is the praise of the armor;
the thirteenth praises the whip, and the fourteenth the hand-guard. (132)
In the first quarter of the fifteenth [chapter], the poisoned arrow (digdheṣu) is praised;
in the second, the iron-tipped one (ayomukhī); and in the latter half, the Vāruṇa weapon.
In the sixteenth [verse], however, the arrow released from his bow is praised;
but in the seventeenth, [the praise concerns] the donning of armor after the commencement of battle and so forth. (134)
The eighteenth is to be known as a hymn of praise; it is the supreme hymn of Yuyutsu. And in its final quarter-verse, the seer invokes blessings for himself. || 135 ||
Having praised the components of battle for those two with this hymn,
the sage then sent them back toward Vāraśikha.
Desiring to assist the king, Bharadvāja praised him with these four verses; gratified by this, Purandara [was pleased].
Having approached Abhyāvartin on the bank of the river Haryaṇyā,
the Lord of Śacī, accompanied by Āyaman, struck them down.
Having conquered Vāraśikha, those two Añjaneyas then returned and presented various kinds of wealth to their preceptor, Bharadvāja.
Bharadvāja and Garga were indeed seen by Indra on the road;
with these [verses], "dvayān prastoka," they both praised that gift. (140)
The seer also praised that gift of his there with a single verse,
himself proclaiming the two-fold gift given to Agni.
However, Rathītara considered that those deities who were mentioned in the hymn by way of incidental reference were indeed the recipients of the hymn during the praise.
Marīci was indeed the son of Prajāpati; his son was the sage Kaśyapa, the offspring of Marīci.
To him there were thirteen wives, daughters of Dakṣa.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Danāyu, Siṃhikā, Muni, Krodhā, Viśvā, Variṣṭhā, Surabhi, and Vinatā. || 144 ||
And he gave Kadrū and Vinatā as daughters to Kaśyapa;
and from them were born the gods, the asuras, the gandharvas, the uragas, and the rākṣasas.
The birds, the Piśācas, and other species were born there;
among them, the goddess Aditi gave birth to twelve sons.
Bhaga, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Mitra, and Varuṇa;
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Vivasvat of great splendor;
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and likewise Indra—the twelfth is said to be Viṣṇu.
From her was born that pair, Mitra and Varuṇa.
While those two Ādityas were at a sacrificial session, they beheld the Apsaras Urvaśī;
their seed was spilled and fell into a *vāsatīvare* jar.
In that very moment, the two powerful ascetics Agastya and Vasiṣṭha were born there as ṛṣis.
Then, when the semen had fallen in many places—in a water-pot, in water, and on the ground—
On the dry land, however, the sage Vasiṣṭha was born, the best of seers. || 151 ||
In the jar, Agastya was born from the water as a highly effulgent fish;
thereafter, the illustrious Agastya rose up, measuring the size of a sacrificial pin (śamyā).
Because he is measured by means of a measure (māna), he is therefore called Mānya here;
or else, because the sage was born from a jar (kumbha) and is indeed measured by a jar as well. 153.
The designation "Kumbha" (the jar) is used for a specific measure;
therefore, while the waters were being drawn out, Vasiṣṭha remained standing upon a lotus. 154.
His name arose from his qualities, for he was the foremost in the act of dwelling;
indeed, he had previously beheld Indra, who is invisible even to the seers, through his ascetic power.
Then Indra, whose vehicle is drawn by bay horses, declared to him the portions pertaining to Soma;
for it is seen in the Brāhmaṇa that the sages indeed said, "Indra. (157)
Vasiṣṭha and the Vasiṣṭhas, the Brāhmaṇas engaged in the work of Brahman,
are likewise the most worthy of sacrificial fees in all rites and sacrifices.

Therefore, if there should ever be members of the Vasiṣṭha lineage among the sacrificial assistants even today, one should honor them with sacrificial fees; for such is this scriptural tradition of the Bhāllaveyas. (159)
The seer Maitrāvaruṇi, with sixteen subsequent hymns, praised Agni; thus, O Agni, be pleased with us here through these propitiatory verses. 160.
First, "pra agnaye," then "pra samrājaḥ" as the second; these three verses beginning with "pra agnaye" are dedicated to Vaiśvānara, while the subsequent ones are dedicated to Indra. (161)
The fifteen hymns beginning with "nipāta" are praises of the Maruts;
however, in the hymn beginning with "nakiḥ sudāsaḥ," there is the description of the gift of Paijavana.
Vasiṣṭha, however, has declared that two [of the four] belong to the grandson.
They declare that the *Saṃvāda* and the *Sūkta* dedicated to Indra are indeed the *Śvityaṅśas*. || 163 ||
In this [section], the greatness, birth, and deeds of Vasiṣṭha and Agastya, along with their sons, as well as their dialogue with Indra, are celebrated.
Thereafter, there are four verses addressed to the Viśvedevas;
among them, one praises Ahi Budhnya with the verse beginning "mā no hiṃsīḥ" and another likewise praises Ahi Budhnya with "mā no 'hiṃ budhnyam. (165)

The word *ahirāhan* refers to the clouds, for he (the Sun) moves among them; that which is the serpent (*ahi*) is the one dwelling in the depths (*budhnya*), for he is born within the *vudhna*, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). 166. May this hymn of Savitṛ rise up; may the deity Vājina bring us peace.
In this context, the Śruti states that "bhaga" is a portion consisting of two verses and half a verse, beginning with the words "bhagam ugram. (167)
And here, the third quarter-verse has the serpent as its deity in the fifth [syllable];
just as Bhaga is in the half-verse of the Ugra [hymn], so indeed is Bhaga also [here]. 168.
For he, Savitṛ, shall indeed bestow jewels; thus he is Bhaga.
These five verses addressed to the Viśvedevas are followed by five verses whose deity is Bhaga. (169)

The final [verse] of the *uṣas* hymn is dedicated to Prātarjit; some, however, consider it to be for the *aśīr* (benediction) here, while others declare that it concerns Bhaga in the verse beginning with "drātaḥ. (170)
The seers proclaim [the deities] at the beginning and at the end according to the context;
however, in this hymn, various other deities also appear therein.

Other deities, however, are celebrated [as such] either because they share the same abode (sālokya), because of their companionship (sāhacarya), or again because of their close association (saṃstava), or because of their position within the divine hosts (gaṇasthāna), or out of devotion (bhakti).
The Dādhika, the Sāvitra, and the Raudra [hymns] follow in successive order;
in the Dādhika, however, the deities of the first [verse] are proclaimed. (173)
Those [verses] are to be known as the Āpas; the first triplet (tṛca) is the Āpya, while the last is declared to be either Vaiśvadevī or Ārbhavī. || 174 ||
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the scripture, that Ārbhava hymn is indeed praised;
on the tenth day, there is the praise of the waters, beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ," in its entirety.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Bṛhaddevatā.
With the hymn beginning "ā mām," the deities are praised verse by verse:
Mitra and Varuṇa, Agni, the gods, and likewise the rivers. (1)
The two triplets have Āditya as their deity; the triplet beginning with "pra" is dedicated to Rodasī; there are four verses for Vāstoṣpati; thus, seven are known as the Prasvāpinīs. || 2 ||
Furthermore, there are four hymns dedicated to the Maruts, beginning with "ka īm". Of these, the final Ṛc praises their father, the god Tryambaka.
In the hymn of praise, however, one should worship Mitra and Varuṇa with seven verses beginning with "yad";
and the two gods, the Aśvins, with eight subsequent verses beginning with "prati vām."
"That which rises today alone until the sun sets" and "three times" constitute four and a half verses;
however, the verse beginning with "That eye of yours" (yadadya) is proclaimed as the deity of the eye.

Regarding the verses for the Ādityas, Śaunaka has stated that two of those verses are for you today; all other verses are dedicated to Sūrya, including those proclaimed as "yadadya" (that which is today). || 6 ||
These verses beginning with "ime cetāraḥ" and so forth are for the sacrificial session (sattra); Mitra is praised as "mitaḥ.
These nine [verses] are recorded for Aryaman, Varuṇa, and also for Mitra. || 7 ||
The ten verses beginning with "yadadya sūra" are remembered as the Ādityas:
Savitṛ, Vāyu, Aditi, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Bhaga. (8)
The three verses beginning with "stutā ud" and "tyat" are dedicated to Sūrya; the teacher Śaunaka has stated that the subsequent verse, "taccakṣuḥ," is a prayer for blessings (āśis). || 9 ||
Uṣas, however, has seven hymns; those following them are for Vyuchantī. Next, the four beginning with "indrāvaruṇā" are a praise of Indra and Varuṇa. || 10 ||
In this half-verse beginning with "udu jyotiḥ," the middle [note] was praised;
there, Vasiṣṭha, while sleeping, wandered from the house of Varuṇa at night.
Then he entered there; as he did so, a barking dog rushed toward him—a howling dog, running and prepared to bite.
Having consoled him with the two verses beginning with "O Arjuna," he caused him to fall lifeless;
he then put that man and the other Varuṇa-like being to sleep.
Then King Varuṇa was bound by his own nooses;
thus bound, he [the seer] praised his father with four subsequent hymns (sūktas).
His father praised him with the hymn "dhīra" and released him from there;
then, when the verse beginning with "dhruvāsu tvā" was recited, the bonds were loosened from him.
The next three *saktas* belong to Vāyu and begin with "pra vīrayā.
Among these, those in which there is praise of two deities are praised as belonging to Indra and Vāyu. (16)
In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, it is stated that the *pra-uga* chant is dedicated to Vāyu and addressed to the heroes;
by transposing the word order, the preeminence of Vāyu is expressed. (17)
By means of that truth, there are three *ṛcas* up to the fourth;
then one more, "uśantastvā," and two for "pra sotaḥ"—these nine are traditionally recorded. (18)

"O Indra and Agni, pure one"—these [two verses] are for Sarasvat; the next two are for Sarasvant; and with the verse "Sarasvant with that... and three verses beginning with "janīyantah," [the offering is made]. || 19 ||
In ancient times, King Āhuṣa, the son of Nahuṣa, intending to undergo initiation for a thousand years,
traveled across this earth on a single chariot, addressing all the rivers flowing toward the ocean.
"I shall sacrifice; carry my portions, either in pairs or one by one.
The rivers replied to that king, "We are of little power; how [could we do so]? (21)
"May we all receive our shares from you in this thousand-fold sacrifice.
Resort to the Sarasvatī; she will lead you there, O son of Nahuṣa. (22)
Having said, "So be it," he went quickly to the river Sarasvatī;
she received him and yielded milk and clarified butter.
The son of Varuṇa recounted this most wonderful deed of Sarasvatī toward the king to the second wife of the first [king].
In the sacrifice, there is [a hymn] for Bṛhaspati and one for Indra; then, in the Vaiṣṇava [section], there are three "uru" verses for Indra, and three further verses for Parjanya.

In this [hymn], the first verse praises Indra, while the second and subsequent verses praise Bṛhaspati; at the sacrifice, the first [verse] praised Indra alone, whereas the final one praised both Indra and Bṛhaspati.
The third and the ninth [verses] praise Indra and Brahmaṇaspati;
for a year, however, they praise the frogs; and that which follows is addressed to Indra and Soma.
Overwhelmed by grief for his son, the sage then beheld that demon-slaying [weapon],
distressed at that time because his hundred sons had been killed by the Saudāsas.
Those [hymns] addressed to Pākaśasana, Ṛk, and Soma are followed by those addressed to Agni;
the eleventh is addressed to the Viśvedevas, and the subsequent two-verse hymn is addressed to Soma. (29)
If it is addressed to Agni, it is "yad vāham"; that which is addressed to Indra is known as "yo me.
That beginning with "pra yā jigāti" is addressed to the pressing-stones (grāvṇī), while "vi tiṣṭhadhvam" is addressed to the Maruts. ||30||

"Pravartaya" [is the first verse]; there are five verses addressed to Indra; the one to Indra-Soma has the *ṛc* as its final verse; the *ṛṣi* invokes a blessing [with the words] "He invokes a blessing for you"; and in the *ṛc* [he says] "Protect us. (3.1)
In both heaven and on earth, he likewise protected himself;
he destroyed those owl-demons and night-stalkers who assumed various forms.
On the fifteenth day of the hymn, and likewise on the eighth, Vāruṇi, his soul overwhelmed by pain and grief, cursed as if lamenting. (33)
When those hundred sons had been slain by Sudās, who had become a Rākṣasa due to a curse, Vasiṣṭha was then deeply distressed; so indeed is the tradition.
Kaṇva and Pragātha, the two sons of Ghora, became the eighth maṇḍala; permitted by their teacher, they dwelt together in the forest. (35)
While the two of them were sleeping there, the younger brother, having placed Kaṇva’s wife’s head upon his own lap, did not realize that he was lying on Kaṇva’s lap. || 36 ||
Desiring to curse him, the enraged Kaṇva, suspecting him of evil,
woke him with his foot as if wishing to consume him with his ascetic power.
Having understood his intention, Pragātha stood with palms joined in reverence and requested both of them to act as his mother and father. (38)
Whether he was Ghaura or Kāṇva,
that sage, accompanied by many of his lineage and others, beheld the eighth maṇḍala.
In the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "mā cid aindrāṇi catvāri anvasya sthūram," an Aṅgirasa woman, dwelling eternally with her husband, offered praise. || 40 ||
Although he was actually a woman, that seer made himself out to be a man; he performed this act of attachment, which is proclaimed by four Ṛg-verses beginning with "Praise my gift. (41)
The hymn of Kāśya Vibhindu is proclaimed with two verses beginning with "śikṣā";
that of Bhoja Pākasthāman is praised with four verses beginning with "yam".
Śākaṭāyana considers the two Pragāthas beginning with "pra" to be dedicated to Pūṣan;
however, Gālava holds that the former is dedicated to Indra and the latter to Pūṣan.
In this [section], regarding the hymns dedicated to Indra, the gift of King Kuruṅga is praised in the final *ṛc* of the final hymn with the words, "A massive wealth. (44)
In the *Dūrāt* hymn of the Aśvins, the thirty-seventh verse, as well as the final half-verse and the final two-verse section, are recorded as praises of Kaśu’s gift. (45)
Śākapūṇi, as well as Bhārmyaśva and Mudgala, consider the hymn to Mahānaindra, addressed with ancient verses, to be a praise of Agni Vaiśvānara. (46)

In this [section] containing the *tṛca* "śatam," the gift by them is remembered as *indira*; furthermore, there are three *māruta* hymns beginning with "pra" and three *āśvina* hymns beginning with "ā naḥ. (47)

The hymn beginning with "ya indra" (RV 2.12) is dedicated to Agni; the six verses beginning with "ya indra" (RV 8.91–96) are dedicated to Indra, but in the penultimate verse of the last [hymn], the deity Vāstoṣpati is praised.
This [hymn] has Aditi as its deity; it is praised by three verses addressed to Aditi—namely the sixth, the fourth, and the seventh—and the eighth verse begins with "uta. (49)
The three—Agni, Sūrya, and Anila—are praised verse by verse with the hymn beginning "śamit";
the praise of Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Mitra is with the *pragātha* beginning "yam". (50)
In the Āgneya section, there is a praise of the royal seer Trasadasyu,
saying that he gave fifty maidens and three times seventy cows.
Likewise, he gave them horses, camels, various garments,
jewels, a dark-brown bull, and Agnisara as their husband.
Having taken a wife and departing, the Ṛṣi reported this to Indra;
and Śakra, the lord of Śacī, was pleased by that hymn of praise.
"O Sage, choose a boon," [the god said]. Bowing low, the sage replied: "O Lord, let me enjoy the fifty daughters of the descendant of Kakutstha simultaneously. (54)
May he grant manifold forms at will, eternal youth, and inexhaustible pleasure;
and may the Śaṅkha-treasure and Padma-treasure never depart from my houses.
"By your grace, may this Viśvakarman construct palaces made of gold and separate flower gardens for each of them, filled with celestial trees. (56)
"Let there be no rivalry with co-wives; let everything be ours," she said.
Then [the seers] recited the Māruta Sūkta beginning with "Come hither," and the subsequent Aindra Sūkta beginning with "We [choose you]. (57)
Together with the descendants of Kaṇva and Sobhari who were performing sacrifices,
they ate barley and various kinds of oblations at Kurukṣetra.
That Ākhu praised Indra, Citra, and Sarasvatī;
with this verse beginning "Indro vā," he manifested his power of generosity. (59)
Out of pride, the king of the mice, his mind filled with great joy,
himself praised the wonderful god-like sage and gave him cows.
The rishi indeed subdued ten million [demons] while offering praise;
then, with a joyful heart, he said to the rishi, "O rishi, I am not worthy of your praise."
Having been born among the animals, he was worthy to praise the deities;
with the final verse he praised them again, and with the *Otyam* hymn, he praised the Aśvins.
"Īḷiṣva"—this [verse] belongs to Agni; "sakhāyaḥ" is for Indra;
and the final triplet beginning with "yathā vāraḥ suṣāmyāḥ" belongs to Uṣas. || 63 ||
But these eight deities together shattered the army:
Uṣas, Indra, Soma, Agni, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati. (64)
"Aṅgiras and Saramā"—these two verses beginning with "tā vām" belong to the latter [section];
first there are nine addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, and twelve follow. (65)
The *varū* verses dedicated to Viśvedevas, which King [Vasu] gave as wealth to the seer,
are celebrated in this triplet concerning Ṛjrāśva, the son of Ukṣaṇyāyana.
The Aśvins, being pleased, granted this to Suṣāman; thus it is said here:
"O you two, yoke the chariot of the Aśvins, and those [verses] which follow are addressed to Vāyu. (67)
The son named Manu, whom Vivasvat obtained from Savarṇā,
he— the Fire-god— proclaimed these five Vaiśvadeva hymns in the Uktha.

Now, these ten two-footed verses beginning with "babhru reka" are praised according to their indicative marks (liṅga), for in them the deities are extolled individually by means of their respective actions. (69)
Wherever the deities are praised according to their respective individual actions and qualities,
that indeed is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice known as "Praise of Individual Actions" (pṛthakkarmastuti).
Among them, the first is addressed to Babhru; the next verse is dedicated to Soma and Agni;
then follow verses dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra, Rudra, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, and the Aśvins.
The ninth [verse] is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa; the tenth is a praise of Atri.
Furthermore, the sacrifices that are proclaimed here in connection with the sacrificer [are also included]. (72)
He who conquers at the Dvṛca sacrifice, the powerful lord of those who sacrifice, being praised—his [offspring] is radiant, a sacrificer at the Dvṛca, and swift even in all four [Vedas]. ||73||
For the two sacrificers, husband and wife, there are five verses concerning the couple;
[the first] beginning with "ā śarma" is for the blessing, the next two are for Pūṣan, and the last is for Mitra and Aryaman. (74)
Varuṇa and the Ādityas are praised here; [the hymns] for Agni are for Agni.
Three hymns beginning with "pra kṛtāni" are dedicated to Indra; beyond these are the others.
Then, in this place, the maiden addressed Indra with feminine pronouns;
for that subduer of Pāka (Indra) had desired her, the daughter of the Dānava.
Out of youthful desire for that very Vyaṃsa, he [Vasiṣṭha] approached his elder sister;
thereafter, he recited the hymn to the Aśvins beginning with "agninā," followed by the hymn to Indra.
The first [hymn] is dedicated to Indra and Agni, the next to Agni; the one after that is dedicated to Indra and Agni, and the next to Varuṇa.
In the final [section], the last [hymn] is dedicated to Varuṇa, while the triplet beginning with "ā vām" is dedicated to the Aśvins. ||78||
These two hymns are dedicated to Agni; after them follow those dedicated to Indra.
Regarding the mare Vaśā, Pṛthuśravas, the son of a maiden, gave her away. ||79||

In this [section], the praise of giving is expressed by means of the verses beginning with "ā saḥ" and so forth; the two Pragāthas addressed to Vāyu, as well as the penultimate verse of the hymn [are also included]. (80)
Mitra, Aryaman, and the Maruts as excellent leaders were praised in the *dvṛca* hymns;
and from the forty-second [hymn], Purandara was pleased with Triśoka. (81)
"Having split the mountain with his thunderbolt, the ten Vasus carried off the cows";
this very Ṛṣi himself declared this in that [verse] beginning with "yaḥ tṛn. (82)
The hymn beginning with "stutā navamyā tvaditira mahī" is dedicated to the Ādityas; the final one may also be for Uṣas; and that beginning with "svādoḥ" is remembered as being addressed to Soma.
The remaining eight hymns belong to seers of fierce splendor.
But here, the twenty-sixth *pragātha* is dedicated to Indra and possesses many deities. || 84 ||
Agni perceived the final [hymn] of Ṛgantu; Agni recited the final verse for Sūrya;
and Praskaṇva bestowed whatever wealth belonged to Pṛṣadhra. (85)
The entire [section] here has been praised by means of the two hymns beginning with "tadūbhūrīt";
both of these belong to Indra, while those following the [hymn] to Agni consist of six [verses].
Bhāguri says that the word *nipāta* means "the giver of the gods. || 86 ||
Yāska considers this [first] triplet to be dedicated to the Viśvedevas; however, that which follows in the hymn beginning with "tyān nu" is considered to have the Ādityas as its deity. (87)
Seeing the fish suddenly in the waters of the Sarasvatī, the fishermen cast their nets, bound them, and threw them from the water onto dry land. (88)
Fearing the fall of their bodies, they praised the sons of Aditi;
then, being pleased, they released them and spoke to them.
"O fishermen, let there be no fear of hunger for you; may you attain heaven"—thus did their mother say, and Aditi was praised there with this triplet beginning with "Utá".
Because of their connection through motherhood, this [goddess] is praised in each of their praises;
with "Aindrāṇyā tvā" she praises the chariot, and with "trīṇi ṛtūn upa me" she praises six [verses]. || 91 ||
In this [section], there are five verses praising the gifts of Kakṣīvat and Aśvamedha; the subsequent ones are praises of Indra, Agni, and the Viśvedevas. (92)
The first half-verse of the *dvṛca* has Śeṣa as its deity;
the [next] hymn is addressed to Agni, while the subsequent one is a praise of the oblations (*havis*). || 93 ||
Milk is seen to be of such a nature among both animals and plants; likewise, in the subsequent hymns dedicated to the Aśvins and Agni, [it is said] "ud ity āśvinam" and "viśo-viśaḥ. (94)
With two verses beginning with "By the Ṛks, I...", the seer himself praises his own self;
having praised himself by means of his own self, he then praises the gift of Śrutarvan. (95)
Because of his connection with Ātmadāna and the great river Paruṣṇī, [the sage] praised Indra with three hymns beginning with "parayā" and "imam nu. (96)

This [hymn] beginning with "ayaṃ kṛtnuḥ," this [hymn] beginning with "idaṃ saumyam," these three [hymns] beginning with "trīṇy āindrāṇi" and the one beginning with "parā gāt," and among those beginning with "nahi," the first Ṛc addressed to the Viśvedevas increased [the sacrifice]. || 97 ||
"Of the gods" (devānām) refers to the verse "The most beloved of the gods," which is dedicated to Agni; the next three verses beginning with "O Aśvins" and "To him" are dedicated to Indra.
In ancient times, there was a maiden named Apālā, the daughter of Atri, who suffered from a skin disease.
Having seen her in the solitude of her father’s hermitage, Indra desired her.
Through her ascetic power, she understood everything that Indra intended;
then, taking a water-pot, she went to the bank of the waters.
Having bitten Soma at the edge of the waters, he praised him with a verse in the forest;
thus, the meaning of this [verse] beginning with "kanyā vāri" was subsequently declared. || 10 1 ||
She pressed the Soma juice into her mouth and summoned Indra with the verse, "He who comes hither" (asau ya eṣi);
and Indra drank it from her mouth.
Having eaten cakes and barley meal from that house, he praised her with Rigvedic verses; she, for her part, addressed him with a triplet of verses.
"O Śakra, make me, whose limbs are faultless, possessed of beautiful hair and fine skin.
Having heard those words of hers, Purandara was pleased by her. 104.
Indra, having cast her through the opening between the cart and its yoke, pulled her out three times; thus she became Sutvaksā (the "well-skin").
Of her, the skin that was struck off first became the porcupine;
the next became the monitor lizard, and the outermost skin became the chameleon.
Yāska and Bhāguri say that this hymn is a historical narrative (itihāsa), while Śaunaka says it concerns a maiden; and as for those [verses] following "pāntam" (RV 8.91.3), they belong to Indra.
The *ārbhavī* is declared to be the best in the *uttara* [portion] of the *Aitareyaka*, because that *ārbhava* is recited during the third *chandoma* day. 1.08.
The story of Soma’s flight from the gods:

The *māruta* hymn is the first, the *gaurīvīta* hymn is the next; following these are six hymns dedicated to Indra. Regarding these, they recount the traditional history (*itihāsa*) in the second hymn.
But Soma, afflicted by the fear of Vṛtra, fled away from the gods.
He stood by the river named Maṃśumatī, facing toward the Kurus;
there Vṛtrahaṇ encountered him alone along with Bṛhaspati.
Seeing them prepared for battle with various weapons, Soma, being greatly cheered by the Maruts, stood firm with his own army. || 11.1 ||
Perceiving Vṛtra approaching with his army, desirous of slaying him,
Bṛhaspati spoke to him as he stood there armed with a bow.
"O Lord, this Soma, the lord of the Maruts, come back to the gods!
Having heard these words of the preceptor of the gods, [Indra] feared Vṛtra and [acted] for no good. (1.13)
He said, "No. Then the powerful Śakra, by force, went to heaven itself and took him away;
there the gods drank the soma from him according to the prescribed rite.
Having drunk [the blood], they slew ninety-nine Daityas in battle; all this is likewise declared in these three verses (ṛcas). 115.
Indra, the Maruts, and likewise Bṛhaspati—these indeed are the deities of the triplet; however, Śaunaka has declared that Indra alone is the deity. || 116 ||
The offering to Indra and Bṛhaspati has been described in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa;
there, the descendant of Bhṛgu perceived Indra through a triplet of verses, thinking, "This is not [the usual] Nema."
Indra was pleased with this two-verse hymn; "Behold me, O Sage!
For he alone praises me," he said, "and there is no other Indra. (1.18)

Having heard that, Indra praised himself with two *ṛc* verses, revealing his identity; and the sage, seeing him, was well-pleased and [praised him] with the two-verse hymn beginning with "viśvettā te."
It praises various deeds and the gift of Indra;
furthermore, there are the Manojavā, the Sauparṇī, the Samudra, and the Vajrasaṃstava.
He praises the goddess Speech, who is all-pervading, with the two verses beginning "That speech... Vṛtra stood scorching these three worlds with his own brilliance. (121)
Indra was unable to slay him; approaching Viṣṇu, he said:
"I shall kill Vṛtra; stand today by my side, having exerted your prowess. (122)
"May the Sky grant me an opening as I raise my thunderbolt!
"So be it," Viṣṇu said, and he made that [opening], and the Sky gave him an aperture.

All this has been declared, O friend, regarding the verse beginning with "viṣṇave. Furthermore, there are four verses beginning with the hymn of Maitrāvaruṇī, starting from the verse "tvam ṛdhak. (124)
The feet of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa are praised; the fourth belongs to all the Ādityas—such is the hymn of praise. (125)

The verse beginning with "parā" has the Ādityas as its deity; "ā ma" is a two-verse hymn (dvṛca) dedicated to the Aśvins; and those dedicated to Vāyu, Sūrya, and Uṣas [refer to] the light or the radiance of the moon and the sun.
The cow is praised by the two Ṛg-verses beginning with "pāvamānī" and "prajā ha";
Agni is praised in the subsequent verse beginning with "tvam agne bṛhat. || 127 ||
"O Agni, go together with the Maruts and the Rudras"—thus says the middle [verse];
or rather, in the first half-verse, "prajā ha," Agni is mentioned here. (128)
In the third quarter, Āditya is [the deity], and in the fourth, Madhyama is praised;
this has indeed been explained in the same way in the *Ruhasya Brāhmaṇa* and the *Aitareyaka*.
In the ninth maṇḍala, Soma is praised as Pavamāna; here in this ninth maṇḍala,
the verses beginning with "pavamānavadāpryaḥ" and "samiddhaḥ" are thus extolled.
In this [hymn], Agni is the subject of the words "āyūṃṣi" (lives) throughout these three verses;
however, in this triplet beginning with "avitā naḥ," he is praised together with Pūṣan.
In this [rite], there are two verses addressed to Agni beginning with "yatte," followed by the Sāvitrī verse beginning with "ubhābhyām," and then the subsequent verse addressed to Agni-Savitṛ.
"May the Vaiśvadevī verses purify me; may the Āgneyī verse [purify] what is dear to me.
These two [verses], "And the higher ones for you," are praises of those who study their own Vedic recitation.
In the Sūkta, Nirukta, and Srakva, Agni is praised as the slayer of Rākṣasas;
he is also called the Sun, the Self, and the Purifier. || 134 ||
The third quarter, however, belongs to the Ārbhavas; it is remembered as "Ṛbhu dhīraḥ.
By means of these three quarters, the three gods are here proclaimed. (135)
Brahmā is said to be among the gods; indeed, by means of these three pairs of verses, either Soma himself is praised, or he is praised like the Sun and like the Self.
While a drought was prevailing, the Lord of Śacī questioned the sages:
"In this great and difficult time, by what means do you sustain yourselves? (137)
The cart, the female spirit (śākinī), the cows, agriculture, the chariot, the forest, the ocean, the mountain, and the king—in this manner we live. (138)
While praising him, the young seer Aṅgiras recited this hymn consisting of various verses in the very presence of the other seers. (139)
Indra said to all of them: "Perform very great austerities;
for without austerity, it is not possible to dispel this hardship. (140)
Then they all indeed performed austerities, desiring to conquer heaven;
thereafter, through their fierce austerity, they uttered the Pāvamānī verses.
Free from envy, studious, obedient, and endowed with austerity, he purifies ten ancestors and descendants of his lineage, as well as himself. (142)
Whatever evil he has committed through mind, speech, body, or food,
he becomes purified from all of that and enjoys the fruit of Vedic study.
The Pāvamānī verses are the Supreme Brahman, the pure and eternal light;
at the end of these Gāyatrīs, one should, with focused mind, perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Whoever meditates upon the purifying [Soma], the ancestors, the gods, and Sarasvatī,
for him the milk, ghee, honey, and water shall flow toward the ancestors.
This collection of one hundred hymns, consisting of fourteen sections, is known as the *Pāvamāna*; it comprises exactly seven *anuvākas*. 146.
Then Trita saw seven Agneya hymns in the tenth Mandala;
the subsequent hymn, beginning with "pra ketunā," was seen by Trishiras, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Six of his *ṛc* verses were dedicated to Agni, while another three were his; with those remaining, he praised Indra, according to our sacred tradition, ending with the words "svaprānta. (148)
For he, Triśiras, the son of an Asura’s sister, who assumed all forms, became the priest of the gods out of a desire to please them. (149)
Indra perceived among the gods that the Ṛṣi had been dispatched by the Asuras;
he then swiftly severed those three heads of his with his thunderbolt. || 150 ||
That which was his drinking of Soma became the Kapiñjala bird;
his drinking of wine became the Kalaviṅka; and his eating of food became the Tittiri.
Then the voice of Brahmā addressed him: "O Śatakratu, you are a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, since you have killed Viśvarūpa after he had sought refuge and turned his face away from you. (152)
The seer Sindhudvīpa himself sprinkled him with the hymn beginning with "āpaḥ" for the purpose of removing that vulgar and sinful defilement. (153)
Yamī, desiring sexual union, was rejected by Yama;
that dialogue between those two, the children of Vivasvat, begins with the words "tado cit" (even then).
In the two Agni-related Havirdhāna sheds, when they are joined and praised here, it is the middle Yama who is praised in the verse beginning with "pareyivāṃsam. (155)
The Atharvans, the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, and the Pitṛs together—these sixty hosts of gods, whose portions are the celestial realms, are praised there. (156)
Yama is seen praised by the Pitṛs and the Aṅgirases;
indeed, he is Vivasvat, his father, mentioned many times in the verses of the mantras. (157)

Yama is praised by the ancestors who are associated with the deceased for whom the funeral rites (saṃskāra) are performed; in the three verses beginning with "prehi prehi," the blessings for the deceased are proclaimed. (158)

For Yama is indeed the divine lord of the ancestors; therefore, he is the recipient of the hymn. In the triplet beginning with "ati drava," there are two dogs; [the verse] "udīratām" refers to that which is beyond the paternal realm. 159.
With the subsequent hymn, however, he describes the ritual in the cremation ground.
Among the ancestors, gods, and asuras, there arose three fires: two for carrying the *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors), and that one named Saharakṣas. || 160 ||
In that regard, the phrase "mā enam" is a praise of Kavyavāhana;
the other [phrases], however, are praises of the divine one and not of the asura.
Tvaṣṭṛ had a twin pair, Saraṇyū and Triśiras;
he himself gave Saraṇyū to Vivasvat.
Then, two sons were born to Vivasvat by Saraṇyū;
both of them were indeed Yamas, but among them, Yama was the elder.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Bṛhaddevatā*.
Having begotten a similar woman while her husband was away, Saraṇyū placed the pair upon her and, having become a mare, departed.
From that [wife] Avijñātā, Vivasvat begot Manu;
he too became a royal sage (rājarṣi), equal to Vivasvat himself in splendor.
Having realized that Saraṇyū had departed in the form of a mare,
he quickly became a horse possessing the same characteristics and went toward Tvaṣṭṛ.
And Saraṇyū, having learned that Vivasvat was in the form of a horse, [followed him].
He approached her for sexual union and mounted her there.
Then, by their forceful union, that semen fell upon the earth;
and that mare, desiring pregnancy, sniffed at that semen.
From the semen produced by the mere act of anger, two youths were born:
Nāsatya and Dasra, who are praised as the Aśvins.
Regarding this ancient legend (itihāsa) concerning the two verses whose deity is Saraṇyū,
Yāska considers that Tvaṣṭṛ [is the deity] for both Vivasvat and Tvaṣṭṛ.
The two feet are sacred to Pūṣan; the two that follow are sacred to Agni;
the third may also be sacred to Pūṣan, while the three that follow after those are [sacred to the Maruts]. (8)
In this [section], there is one Ṛg-verse praising the waters; following the Sārasvata triplet, Soma is praised in the indirect manner in the two subsequent triplets beginning with "drapsa. (9)
The blessing of the water-deities, or the verse beginning with "payasvatī," and those four [verses] following it are hymns of praise to Death; they are prescribed for the final ritual act.
From those who remain after the deceased, he prays for long life again;
from those who are living, he prays for this [long life] during the rite of placing the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Just as [he says] "May Dhātrī, Uttarā, and Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter, and then all these other women," he invokes this blessing for women during the rite of applying collyrium.
With the verse beginning "Rise up, O woman," the wife ascends after the deceased;
a younger brother, having recited this, prevents her from doing so. (13)
The Hotṛ priest should perform this rite if there is no brother-in-law (devara);
for according to the injunction of the Brāhmaṇas, there shall be no following of the deceased by the widow. || 14 ||
This duty of women may or may not apply to other castes as well.
For the sake of pacification, one should recite the *Dhanurmantra* while taking up the bow;
for these [mantras] are employed at the cremation ground during the funeral rites for the deceased. (15)
Therefore, one should declare the deity of this triplet to be Death itself;
for when mantras are unexpressed, one should declare the deity according to the ritual action.
For when mantras are unexplained, one should declare their deity according to the ritual action.
In the absence of Prajāpati, [the rites] are performed through mantra and action;
and among those four others mentioned here, one should approach the earthly [goddess] with the words "upa sarpa. (17)
The application of these [rites] occurs during the collection of the bones of the deceased;
on each successive day, having removed the other [bones], [the rite is performed]. 18.
With the final blessing, "May the ancestors bestow [blessings] upon me during the days," he prayed;
and they have sustained me with life as I proceed through the days yet to come. (19)
Some, however, know that "ni vartadhvam" refers to cows and water;
the first half-verse belongs to Agni, while the latter belongs to Soma. || 20 ||
The sixth [verse] belongs to Indra; on the second day, both deities are invoked.
The ten-syllable mental hymn (mānasa-sūkta) is said to be for the purpose of pacification. || 21 ||

Three [hymns] are dedicated to Indra; among them, those following the two addressed to Agni are the three-verse hymn dedicated to the Aśvins, while "yuvam" is the last of those dedicated to Indra. (22)
The first [verse] is auspicious and gentle, belonging to Pūṣan; the three following belong to Indra.
Being intoxicated by the first of these, he praises his own deeds. (23)
How he moves among living beings, how he rains, and how he protects—all this has been declared in this hymn by means of eight verses beginning with "abhūr iti. (24)
With "saptā" he praises the Maruts; with the subsequent verse beginning with "vajram," he praises Indra; and with "pīvānam," he worships Agni, Indra, and Soma as the fat ram. || 25 ||
The first half-verse and the latter [half-verse] of that [hymn] refer to Parjanya together with Vāyu;
"vi krośanāsaḥ" refers to Agni, while the subsequent [verse] refers to Sūrya alone.
"etau me 'yam yaḥ," "ityete," and "stutiścaivendravajrayoḥ";
then "vṛkṣe-vṛkṣe dhanuḥ" and "indraṃ devānām"—these are three [hymns]. (27)
The rain-clouds, the wind, and the sun are the givers of cold, heat, and rain; and at the end, both the sun and the wind are praised together in that state.
In this verse beginning with "sā te jīvātu," either Indra or indeed Sūrya is addressed;
for the rest of the dialogue belongs to both the seer and Śakra.
The even-numbered verses are to be known as belonging to Śakra, while the other verses belong to Vasukra.
Having seen the gods arrive, the daughter-in-law of Indra observed that Śakra had not yet come. (30)
"My father-in-law spoke of the sacrifice as if it were out of sight; he has not yet arrived.
If he were to come, he would eat the parched grain and even drink the Soma. (31)
Having heard her words, Vajradhṛk arrived at that very moment;

"With the third and the fourth [verses], 'pra devatrā' and so forth, in the praise of the waters. (32)
By this name, "Apāṃnapāt," the middle Agni is praised. || 33 ||
That which is the Vaiśvadeva [sūkta], after it has departed, the Aindra follows;

While [the king] was honoring Kuruśravaṇa, two others [honored] Trāsadasyava;
when King Mitrātithi had died, the seer [protected] his grandson from his enemies.
He [Indra] caused Upamaśravas to grieve with four [hymns];
that which is the hymn beginning with "prāvepāḥ" is called the praise of Akṣa. (36)

In this [hymn], the twelfth verse praises the dice; the seventh, beginning with the ninth, praises agriculture and instructs the gambler. The remaining verses, dedicated to the Viśvedevas, censure the dice as something truly senseless.
Some consider this [hymn] to be dedicated to Savitṛ; others regard it as the supreme praise of the great Agni.
The teachers Śaunaka, Yāska, and Gālava, however, hold the final verse to be the most excellent. (38)
Salutation to the hymn dedicated to Sūrya and Indra; in this Sūrya hymn, those verses which are praised as sixty are the "Nipātinyaḥ" (the falling ones) at the end of the Sūkta.
Here, however, there is a Dvṛca (pair of verses) dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
The three [verses] addressed to the Aśvins are indeed excellent, as are those addressed to Indra;
however, in the final verse among those addressed to Indra, Bṛhaspati is praised in the half-verse. || 40 ||
On the following day, at the Āgneya [stotra], Dyāvāpṛthivī and the Viśvedevas are praised with the final verse of the first [stotra], by pādas and by half-verses respectively. || 41 ||
In former times, Ghoṣā, the daughter of Kakṣīvat, was unfortunate due to a malignant disease;

She fell into deep reflection: "Neither my son nor my husband is here;
therefore, O Lords of Auspiciousness, I shall in vain resort to old age. (43)
Just as these two, O dear one, having propitiated me, obtained youth, long life, health, and sovereignty, which is like poison in the hands of all beings.
If I am his daughter, may I too possess the good fortune of those who are beautiful;

Regarding the two hymns beginning with "cintayanti," she who perceived you both—those two Aśvin deities were pleased by her praise—and for her, there was an opening of fortune. (46)
Having entered, the two of them made her free from old age and disease and endowed with good fortune;
they gave her a husband and a son, the sage Suhastin.
They gave it to the two Suparṇas, which is celebrated as "yan nāsatyā";
and to Ghoṣā, the daughter of Kakṣīvat, yet by this [hymn] she did not become free from old age.
The daughter of Prajāpati was named Vikuṇṭhā;
she, desiring a son equal to Indra, then performed very great penance. (49)
She then received various boons and ritual powers from Prajāpati;
and from her, Indra himself was born, desiring to conquer the Daityas and Dānavas.
Once, he engaged in battle with the Dānavas;
he slew ninety-nine and seven times seven of them.

Having shattered the cities made of gold, silver, and iron by the strength of his own arms, and having slain all those situated upon the earth and other realms according to their respective places; ||52||
On earth he destroyed the Kālakeyas and the archers among the Paulomas, and in heaven he exterminated those sons of Prahlāda.
Having obtained the kingdom among the Daityas, he, arrogant due to his own prowess and deluded by the illusion of the Asuras, began to oppress the gods.
But being oppressed by that asura of immeasurable power,
they fled toward Saptagu, the best of rishis, in order to awaken him.
There was a sage named Saptagu who was his dear friend; he praised him, touching his hand, with the words "jagrbhma. (56)
Then, having realized his own self and being delighted by the hymn of seven verses, he praised himself with three [verses] beginning with "I am the earth. (57)
Proclaiming his own deeds which he had performed in the past,
[he told how] he had made the Vaideha king Somapi one-shouldered.
In ancient times, the king of Videha became such through the curse of Vasiṣṭha;
yet, by the grace of Indra, he performed sacrificial sessions (sattra) such as the Sārasvata and others.
Through this [hymn] beginning with "pra vo mahas," one attains abundant power, the warding off of even enemies,
sovereignty over all men, and lordship over the worlds,
as well as inexhaustible personal valor.

When his brothers were sacrificed into the fire by means of the *vaṣaṭ* call—into Vaiśvānara, the lord of the household, the youngest Agni, and the purifier; and when Saha was born from the fire—|| 61 ||
"The Agni Saucika departed from the gods," so says the Śruti.
Having withdrawn, he entered the seasons, the waters, and the trees.
Then, when the fire that carries oblations had vanished, the Asuras appeared;
but the gods, having slain the Asuras in battle, looked only for Agni.
Yama and Varuṇa both beheld him from afar;
taking hold of him together, they both went toward the gods.
Having seen him, the gods said: "O Agni, carry our oblations;
accept boons from us, O Citrabhānu, and favor us. Being well-disposed yourself, make the paths leading to the gods easy to traverse. (65)
Then Agni replied to them: "O Viśvedevas, I shall do exactly what you have told me; may the five classes of beings accept my office as Hotṛ."
The fire at the entrance of the hall, the consecrated fire, the son of the householder, the northern fire, and the southern fire—these are remembered as the five persons. || 67 ||
Humans, ancestors, gods, Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas;
Gandharvas, ancestors, gods, Asuras, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. || 68 ||
Yāska and Aupamanyava have stated these [five]; Śākaṭāyana considers the castes (varṇas) to be five, with the Niṣādas as the fifth.
But Śākapūṇi considers them to be the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the sacrificer (yajamāna).
They say that these are the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Udgātṛ, and the Brahmā.
The eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the vital breath—these are the proponents of the self (ātman).

Indeed, in the Aitareya [Brāhmaṇa], serpents and Brāhmaṇas are mentioned;
as well as others born of the earth, and other gods worthy of sacrifice.
May my life be long, may there be various oblations,
and may there be safety for my elder brothers at every sacrifice.

May the *prayājas* and *anuyājas*, the clarified butter, and the animal sacrifice offered with the *soma*—all these indeed have me as their deity; and may the sacrifice itself have me as its presiding divinity. (74)
"O Agni, yours is the sacrifice"—this is the response; and he is the Sviṣṭakṛt [offering] for whom there are three thousand and nine hundred [verses]. (75)
And all thirty-three gods indeed granted every boon;
then Agni, cheerful and pleased, was placed at the forefront by the Viśvedevas.
Having shaken off his limbs during the sacrifices, the tireless Havyavāhana,
the divine-souled carrier of oblations, performed the office of the Hotṛ priest together with his brothers, being well-pleased.
Her bones were devadāru wood; her fat and flesh were guggulu resin;

In this context, praise is also seen both as being like the vital breath (prāṇa) and like the self (ātman).
These two [verses] belong to the Vaiśvadeva hymn, while the second triplet belongs to the Manas hymn.

Listen to this well-spoken discourse, joined with a narrative, which I desire to tell you—
concerning one who has lost his senses through delusion and has been struck down by an enemy.
Whether it be the livelihood of Subandhu’s living beings, or the praise of your mind, King Atiratha of the Ikṣvāku line [honored] his domestic priests with chariots and horses. 85.
Having cast out those of two-footed lineage within the circle of Atri, beginning with his kinsmen,
there were then two deceitful twice-born men named Kirātākulī.
Asamāti placed those two most excellent ones at the front, for he held them in high regard;
those two doves, having become birds, went toward the Gopāyanas. (87)
Through the power of illusion and through yoga, they both rushed toward Subandhu;
he, from grief and from the blow, fainted and fell.
Then, having snatched away his life-force, the two approached the king;
thereafter, when Subandhu had fallen and was lifeless, the three brothers [acted].

The Gaupāyanas together recited the *svastyayana* hymn beginning with "May all [be well] for me," while they approached him with the hymn that begins with "yad" for the purpose of turning his mind back. || 90 ||
And one should mutter for the sake of medicine that which carries one beyond [misfortune];
therein, the first triplet of the hymn is the dispeller of Nirṛti. || 91 ||
The first three quarters [of the verse] beginning with "mo ṣu" belong to Soma, while the last is Nairṛta;
