The *tṛcas* beginning with "śam it rodasī" are for the sake of pacifying Subandhu alone; they are not prescribed for the *ṛc*. The half-verse beginning with "sam it" is addressed to Indra within that same *ṛc*.
Then, for the sake of destroying *rapas*, they praised the two worlds (*rodasī*);
for the term *rapas* is said to denote both sin and suffering. (95)
Then, with four *ṛg* verses, they praised the descendant of Ikṣvāku;
having lauded him with the verse beginning "O Indra, in sovereignty," they pronounced their blessings.
And their mother praised that king, saying, "Of Agastya";
thus praised, the king stood bashfully before the Gopāyanas. (97)
They praised Agni with a hymn in two-footed verses, just as they had done with three-footed ones;
then Agni spoke to them: "These have passed within the sacrificial enclosures."
And for this Subandhu, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, the Fire-god—seeking his welfare and having protected him—gave back his life to Subandhu and said, "Live! (99).
Praised by the Gaupāyanas, he departed for the third heaven in delight;
thinking "This is our mother," they joyfully called out to Asu, the son of Subandhu.
Not even for a moment is it satisfied. || 100 ||
Having pointed out Subandhu’s body fallen upon the earth,
they sang the remainder of his well-spoken verses in order to steady his consciousness.
Thinking "he has regained his life," they touched her separately with their hands;
on the second day, there were Vaiśvadeva offerings and a hymn of praise to the Aṅgirases. ||102||
By proclaiming his birth, his deeds, and his friendship with Indra, the hymns beginning with "pra nūnam" offer praise to Sāvarṇya Manu. (103)
For the sake of that very longevity, the seer approached and praised the gods;
"Sutrāmāṇam," "Mahīm ū ṣu," and "Dakṣasya" are the praises of Aditi.
"May there be well-being from the wholesome; indeed, may there be well-being through the praise of the Maruts.
For it is stated in the Ādhvaryava texts: "One recites a verse addressed to the Maruts. (105)
That which is "the cow" (gaur) is praised as such; it is the intermediate speech (madhyamā vāk).
The verse for Mitra is addressed to Mitrā-Varuṇa, and that for Bhujyu from distress is addressed to the Aśvins. 1.06.
He also praises Manu with the *svasti* hymn and the middle *vāc*;
then these two [verses] belonging to Bṛhaspati, the *bhadrā*, and the *āpriya*s for Agni. || 107 ||
In the first half-verse of the Bārhaspatya hymn, Brahmaṇaspati [spoke];
then Bṛhaspati praised that knowledge with a Sūkta.
The employment of mantras for the sake of livelihood is prohibited;
for here, one generally observes the true knowledge of the essential meaning of the Vedas. (110)
Some teachers say that here there is praise of those skilled in speech; for just as one who knows no meaning is censured by some verses and yet feasts on others, so it is here. (111)
How the wise ones discovered her while she was dwelling among the Ṛṣis, and how they distributed her at the sacrifice—all that has been described here in the third [chapter]. (112)
On the tenth day, however, the learned one is praised with the final *ṛc*;
he has declared the application of the great officiating priests (*mahartvij*) and their ritual duties within the sacrifice.
Others, however, praise Dakṣa and the eight sons of Aditi:
Dhātṛ, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aṃśa, Sūrya, Aryaman, and Bhaga. (1.14)
In the two hymns beginning with "aindre" and "pra su," that which follows [the first] is as follows:
there, the rivers flowing eastward, westward, and southward [are mentioned]. (1.15)
These seven [hymns] are primarily praised in groups of seven;
among them, two are addressed to the Maruts, beginning with "ā vo" and "abhrapruṣaḥ."
In the Āgneya [section], "apaśyam"; in the Vaiśvakarmaṇa, "ya imā"; in the Mānyava, "yaste"; and that which follows, "mama vrate. (117)
Then, Parāśara, the son of Agni, praises all the celestial dwellers with abundant blessings, beginning with the verse "yad ud it" which consists of eight verses. (118)
Among them is a verse dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa; the fourth is that of Indra and Agni, followed by one for Savitṛ and Sūryā, who is indeed the wife of Vivasvat. (1.19)
She who is praised as Vṛṣākapāyī and is called Uṣas—this Dawn goes forth, having divided herself threefold, toward her lord. 120.
Having become Uṣas before sunrise, and Sūryā when the sun stands at midday,
she becomes Vṛṣākapāyī at the ends of the days and departs.
In this context, the Ṛgveda verse beginning with "sauryā" refers to Satya, Sūrya, Ṛta, and Soma;
however, by means of the three subsequent verses, the plant Soma is described.
The last Ṛg among these clearly praises the Moon;
however, the state of Sūryā’s feelings is expressed by the eight verses beginning with "Raibhī. (123)
When he praises the Aśvins with a *dvṛca*, he thereby praises Sūrya with the latter [verse].
The seventeenth [verse] belongs to the Viśvedevas; the following one is dedicated to Sūrya and Candra.
In this [hymn], the first two quarters of the subsequent [verse] belong to Sūrya and the latter two to Candra;
however, Aurṇavābha considers the Aśvins to be praised in this two-verse hymn.
For they are indeed the sun and the moon, and they are remembered as the prāṇa and apāna breaths;
they alone are day and night, and they alone are heaven and earth.
For those two pervade the worlds with light and with essence;
they move separately, by way of the south and by way of the north.
The Sun moves among living beings; he indeed impels them well. For the sake of their excellent movement, he proceeds among them, coordinating all their activities.
He moves beautifully, or he moves as one who is worthy of being sought;
having first gathered [the materials], the Moon then fashions them.
In this [hymn], the verse beginning with "sukiṃśukam" praises Sūryā as she ascends to her husband;
and in the subsequent two-verse hymn, it praises the Gandharva Viśvāvasu.
With this verse, "anṛkṣarā," the husband and wife praise their journey here; but with the following five verses, he praises the bride as she enters the house.
They declare that the granting of garments and of brides as a boon occurs when there is the loss of a woman's affection for her husband, provided there is the means to give clothing. (132)

Except for sexual intercourse with her husband, the abduction [of a woman] is forbidden; those two verses which praise the destroyers of consumption (yakṣmanāśin) [are recited] against waylayers. 1.33.
He says to her, "May this be auspicious for you," according to what kind of bride's garment she deserves;
and he offers various blessings and instructions to her kinsmen.
A woman who is bound and whose disposition is directed toward worldly existence is here called "dependent on another.
"I grasp your hand with a *ṛc*-verse, grasping the blessings of wealth," [so it is said]. (1.35)

He prays for blessings for the sake of union with her by means of that [first] supreme [prayer]; and he also prays for blessings by means of other supreme [prayers], both separately from those two and together with them. (136)
The first triplet is addressed to Agni; for the next two [verses], there are two [verses] each beginning with "samidhā";
"ā naḥ prajāpateḥ" is addressed to Prajāpati; and the final one is addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati. || 137 ||
For these mantras are declared to belong to men as well;
they are specifically categorized according to their form as those for the officiating priest (ārtvija) and those for the sacrificer (yājamāna). 138.
In this [rite], whichever deities are celebrated in each verse (pratyṛcam), one should name that deity in those [verses]; or one may name the Nārāśaṃsa [deities]. || 139 ||
The *auṣasī* [verse] is in every respect said to be filled with emotional states (*bhāva*);
in this hymn (*sūkta*), it is observed along with the *sūryā* [verse], and even a quarter-verse (*pāda*) is found here. (140)
For this hymn belongs to Vārṣākapa, and that Kapila is indeed Indra, the bull;
and Prajāpati is also Indra—Indra is superior to all. (141)
The section beginning with "rakṣohaṇ" praises the three fires pertaining to Agni—the supreme oblation, this middle one, and that which is Vaiśvānara. (142)
From Indra [he received] that which was attached to Puruṣa, and from the final [verse] of the Pauruṣa [hymn];
the manner in which the Sādhyas partook of him for the sake of sacrifice—that is what is called "artha" (the purpose). || 143 ||
In this [verse], Soma is seen here as being praised in an Indra-hymn with the words "āpāntamanyuḥ";
or rather, it is Soma himself who is praised, either because of his shared world (sālokya) or because of his association (sāhacarya). 144.
And Rathītara declared that Soma also shares in this [classification], for Agni is praised here along with Indra in the *nipāta* hymns by Aruṇa. (145)
Regarding that which follows the verse "He who indeed departs from the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice," he there worships the pressing-stone as if it were a personified being.
With the two Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "pra tad duḥsīma," he praises the gift of kings.
Formerly, the Apsaras Tūrvashī dwelt with the royal sage Purūravas after making an agreement; she lived with him and practiced righteousness. (147)
Likewise, Indra, the subduer of Paka, observed his [the child's] dwelling with those who were not his peers,
as well as his devotion to the Grandfather [Brahmā], which was equal to that of Indra himself.
To bring about their separation, he spoke to Vajra, who stood at his side:
"O Vajra, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, break the affection between those two.
Saying "So be it," Vajra shattered their love through his own illusory power.
Then, deprived of her, the king wandered like one insane. || 150 ||
While wandering by the lake, he saw a woman as beautiful as Urvaśī herself,
surrounded on both sides by five equally beautiful female companions.
He said to her, "Come back! But she spoke to the king out of distress:
"Having failed to reach me here today by you, you shall obtain me again in heaven. (152)
Regarding the invocation and the narrative, Yāska considers this to be a dialogue between two parties, whereas Śaunaka regards it as an *itihāsa* (historical narrative). 153.
"Haya" is the supreme mantra of Indra; "pra te yā oṣadhīḥ" and "tavaḥ" are for the application of medicines. This serves as a means for the destruction of consumption (yakṣman). || 154 ||
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa Devāpi and Śaṃtanu Kauravya—these two brothers became princes among the Kurus. (155)
Of those two, Devāpi was the elder and Śaṃtanu the younger;
however, that prince Śaṃtanu, the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, suffered from a skin disease.
When their preceptor had gone to heaven, they invited the subjects to accept the kingdom;
having reflected for a moment as it were, he replied to those subjects.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Bṛhaddevatā.
"I do not deserve the kingdom; let Śāntanu be your king.
Having said, "So be it," those subjects consecrated Śāntanu for the sovereignty.
Then, after the Kauravya had been consecrated, Devāpi entered the forest;
thereupon, Parjanya did not rain for twelve years throughout the kingdom.
Then Śāntanu, together with his subjects, went to Devāpi and sought to appease him regarding that transgression of dharma.
Then, together with the subjects, he [the king] sought to entice him with the kingdom;
but Devāpi, standing bowed with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him.
"I am not worthy of the kingdom, as my senses are impaired by a skin disease;
nevertheless, O King, I myself shall perform for you the sacrifice for rain."
Then Śantanu appointed him as his domestic priest for the office of the officiating priest;
and he performed his ritual duties during the rainy season according to the prescribed rules.
With the *ṛc* verses beginning with "bṛhaspate prati," he sacrificed to Bṛhaspati;
and by means of the second verse of this hymn, he was awakened by Jātavedas.
"I place a radiant speech within your mouth; praise the deities.
Then, being pleased with him, he granted him divine speech, and he likewise did so.
With four *ṛc* verses he sang to the gods for the sake of rain alone;
with the remainder of the hymn, to Agni; and with the subsequent hymn, to Indra. (9)
"O Indra, be firm"—this is the supreme praise of all the officiating priests (ṛtviks);
the application of this [hymn] here is proclaimed through the manifestation of their power. (10)
Śākaṭāyana considers it to be a hymn (sūkta) concerning the deceased and the Itihāsas;

however, because they are the givers of the dakṣiṇās, the Bhojas are praised with four [verses].
The Asuras known as Paṇis, who dwell beyond the Rasā river, carried off the cows of Indra and concealed them with great effort.

then the subduer of Pāka dispatched Saramā there as a messenger.
Then the Paṇis, the Asuras, questioned her with uneven-numbered verses: "From where do you come?

seeking you and the herd, I am inquiring after the cows for Indra. (27)
Knowing her to be Indra’s messenger, the evil-minded Asuras said to her: "O Saramā, do not [take] our cows; become our sister here. (28)
Then, being filled with devotion, we shall divide the portion of cattle;

She said, "I do not desire sisterhood or wealth;

The Asuras, having said "So be it," then took that milk;

Then, having consumed that supreme, heart-pleasing elixir which bestows strength and nourishment,

On the far side of which was their city, exceedingly difficult to conquer;
and Indra asked Saramā, "Have you seen the cow?"
She replied "No" to Indra, but due to the power of the Asura,
he became enraged and struck her with his foot as she was then disgorging milk.
Agitated by fear, she returned once more toward the Paṇis;
meanwhile, Indra, whose vehicle is drawn by green horses, followed her tracks on his chariot.
Having gone there, he slew the Paṇis and brought back those cows;

The other three [verses] belong to Varuṇa; the final quarter-verse belongs to Indra alone.
I am the Vāk-sūkta of Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa.
That hymn to the Viśvedevas beginning with "This night is not mine" is not as excellent as your hymn to the lightning, which is supreme in its benediction.
That which our enemies fashion as a means for their own destruction through sorcery—

The *Keśi* hymn, the *Agni* hymn, the *Kaiśina* hymn, and the *Sūkta*, as well as whatever follows; here the first [hymn] belongs to the gods, and the subsequent triplet belongs to Vātadeva. (49)

Indra was the nipāta "Apehi" (Go away), Agni was "Duḥsvapnaghna" (Destroyer of bad dreams),

The two seers, Gāyina and Bhārgava, beheld for you the [hymn] addressed to Indra;

The deities mentioned there were praised in the third verse; with the following verse beginning "vātasya," he praised his own father, Anila. ||71||

"Bestow upon this woman, who desires a son, an embryo that shall be male;
for she considers this union of blessings with all her heart. (84)
Māṭhara maintains that the letter *e* is used in a name for the sake of compassion;

The *māhitra* hymn, which they know to be the great praise of the three Ādityas—specifically for Varuṇa among the Ādityas and for the others as well—is [to be recited]. (86)

the Anuṣṭubhs belong to Soma, and the Bṛhatīs to Bṛhaspati. || 105 ||

Those [metres] which belong to a specific deity may have either that deity or Vāyu as their presiding divinity;
however, whichever are *aticchandas* (exceeding the standard metres), those have Prajāpati as their deity.
The Vāyavya mantras are of various meters and are measured by feet; all the Pauruṣya mantras consist of two feet, while those of Brahmā are recorded as having one foot each.
All the Ṛgvedic verses are dedicated to Agni, the Yajurvedic formulas to Vāyu, the Sāmavedic chants to Sūrya, as are all the Brāhmaṇas.
The *vaiśvadeva* is the *vaṣaṭkāra*, the *hiṃkāra*, and the *ye yajāmahe*;

The salutation to the gods and the ancestors, as well as the *svadhā* exclamation, should be known as uttered from the head; it is palatal and possesses the first vowel. (11.2)
The second [place] is between the eyebrows; the third is located at the ear;

the fourth should be at the tip of the nose. That which is produced from the chest is called *mandra*. One praises the *atisvāra* when it is joined with the drawing out (*karṣaṇa*) of the *mandra*. || 113 ||
The deities utter the *kruṣṭa* note; humans, the first (*prathama*) note;
all animals, the second (*dvitīya*) note; and the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the [next] note. 114.
Birds born from eggs and serpents consume the fourth;
the Piśācas, Rakṣasas, and Asuras consume the *mandra*. || 115 ||
But the *atisvāra* tone belongs to all things, both moving and stationary;
it is the *vaiśvadeva* tone, the *kruṣṭa*, which eternally resides in the head.
The first tone of the Sāmans is palatal, has Āditya as its deity, and is the second tone of the Sādhyas; it rests in the region of the eyebrows.
The third note here is that of the Aśvins, which resides in the ears;
the fourth here is that of Vāyu, which is said to be the nasal note.
The fifth tone is declared to be Cākṣuṣa, having the Sun as its presiding deity;
that which is the sixth Sāman tone is Saumya and is called Mandra.
When the *mandra* [register] is joined with a drawn-out [prolongation], it is called *atisvārya*;
that should be known as belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa, being established in the *mandra* position. (120)
Of the seven notes of the Sāman chants, these three gods are said to reside here; however, for the other three notes, there are three lords of the worlds.

however, because they are proclaimed beforehand by means of the Hiṅkāra and the Praṇava. (123)
Thus, one who knows the deities should perceive the deity of the mantras, both individual and collective, in the performance of all ritual acts.
The Seven Sages, the Vasus, and the gods, the Atharvans, the Bhṛgus, Soma, and the Sun;
Pathyā Svasti, the two worlds (Rodasī), and those mentioned in the mantra—Kuhū, Gungū, Aditi, Dhenu, and Dhenyā.
Asunīti, Ilā, Āptyā, Vidhātṛ, and Anumati—these deities, together with the Aṅgirases, are the ones for whom the mantras have been recited. 126.
Vaiśvānara, Suparṇa, Vivasvat, Prajāpati, Dyaus, Sudhanvan, Nagohya,
Apāṃnapāt, Aryaman, and Vātajūti.
And also Ilaspati and Rathaspati. || 127 ||
The Ṛbhus, Parjanya, the mountains, the divine wives, Dakṣa, Bhaga, the quarters of space,
the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the ancestors.

The deities have been enumerated as recipients of hymns and recipients of oblations; they are indicated in both ways by means of particles.

There is no mantra that is not directly perceived by a seer.
Those deities who are to be worshipped in their entirety must be served through yoga, skill, self-restraint, intelligence, extensive learning, austerity, and disciplined observances.
He who knows the Ṛg-verses knows the gods;

Whenever one who knows the deities of the mantras performs a ritual action, the deities partake of his oblation;
they do not partake of that of one who does not know the deities.
For a deity does not accept an oblation that is offered without being made known;
therefore, having mentally established the deity, one should offer the oblation. 132.

He who, being pure, studies his own recitation (svādhyāya) while knowing the mantras and their deities, dwells in heaven as if at a sacrificial session (sattra), and is not oppressed even by those engaged in sacrificial sessions.
This is the rule regarding the recitation (japa), the fire-oblation (homa), the sage (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity (daivata);
for one who employs them otherwise, he is deprived of the fruit thereof.

The knowledge of the seers, meters, deities, and so forth, which is heard in connection with sacrifices and other rites—relying upon that, one should understand that the view of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is enjoined here. (1.35)
He who teaches or even recites [a mantra] without knowing the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), the deity (daivata), and the application (yoga), becomes a sinner. || 136 ||
"In ancient times, the sages, desiring wealth, invoked the deities with Vedic hymns; thus the great seers have declared that you are among the meters. (137)
One should first state the seer (ṛṣi), immediately after that the meter (chandas), and then the deity of the mantras; such is the Vedic injunction regarding ritual actions. (138)
Having discerned within himself the Self as both the pervasive support and the supportless,
one who perceives the auspicious junction should recite the verses concerning the deities.
He enters that supreme light—the immortal Brahman, the eternal source of both the existent and the non-existent, the Lord of the universe, who is both the great and the subtle. || 140 ||
